ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against varying proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Extend the Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) framework by augmenting it with an ensemble-based approach, where multiple ORPO instances are trained on different proxy rewards drawn from a set of candidate proxies with varying assumed correlations. At inference time, the final policy is the average of the individual policies. This approach aims to robustify ORPO against worst-case performance when the proxy reward could be any reward consistent with the correlation constraint.
CONTROLS: ORPO baseline on a single proxy reward, ablation study with a single ORPO instance
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This ensemble-based ORPO approach should outperform the baseline and single-ORPO-instance ablation study, as it leverages the diversity of proxy rewards to reduce vulnerability to high-bad-proxy scenarios; however, its performance may degrade if the candidate proxies are highly correlated, leading to overfitting or underfitting issues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feature-regularized ORPO for improved interpretability
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of ORPO that incorporates feature regularization to improve interpretability. This can be achieved by imposing an L1 or L2 regularization term on the policy's action-values, which encourages simple and sparse features to be used. This regime is dubbed Feature-regularized Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FORPO). By enhancing the interpretability of the learned policies, FORPO is expected to facilitate model-agnostic interpretability and explainability techniques.
CONTROLS: ORPO baseline with and without feature regularization
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FORPO should yield policies with better interpretability compared to ORPO, as evidenced by higher feature sparsity, more transparent action-values, and better alignment with human-expert decision-making patterns; however, its regularization strength should be carefully tuned to avoid over-simplification or under-expression of relevant features.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised version: Clamping-based regularization for more transparent policies in feature-regularized ORPO
PROPOSAL: In the feature-regularized ORPO (FORPO) framework, modify the regularization term to implement a clamping scheme that bounds the activation values of the policy's action-values, further enforcing sparsity and promoting human-interpretable features. Specifically, apply a ReLU clamping to the Q-values by subtracting the minimum non-zero value of Q-values from the entire Q-value space, which creates a "soft" L0 penalty on features and yields more transparent and actionable decision-making criteria.
CONTROLS: ORPO baseline with and without feature regularization, plus ablation study comparing different clamping schemes (e.g., hard vs. soft clamping)
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This clamping-based regularization should improve the interpretability and actionability of FORPO policies even further, fostering specific and handwritten rules that mimic expert-level decision-making patterns; however, its effectiveness may be scenario-dependent and sensitive to hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: From abstraction to concretization: Using prior knowledge in reward learning
PROPOSAL: Incorporate prior knowledge about the reward structure into the reward-hacking mitigation strategy. Develop a neural network-based abstraction layer that maps the true reward to a more interpretable proxy reward. The proposed framework, TRRPO ( Transfer-informed Reward Regularization Policy Optimization), leverages the abstract proxy reward in a trust-region tightening scheme, driven by a novel objective that injects spatial prior knowledge to improve robustness and generalization to unseen situations. By augmenting the RL objective with spatial priors, TRRPO disentangles the true reward structure and subspace exploration from the abstract proxy representation, ultimately leading to better values acting on working policies that achieve objectives historically close to the ground truth (goal excess upper bound).
CONTROLS: ORPO baseline, TRRPO with and without spatial prior knowledge
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TRRPO should exhibit robustness against proxy collapse and reduced exploration-exploitation trade-offs, utilizing the benefits of transfer learning, organized as from prior to supervised-based grafting, yielding significant gains across experiments, assuming well-established mathematical decomposition tools embody the spatial subsystem ϕ used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust monotonic policy learning for scalable value functions
PROPOSAL: Develop a monotonic policy learning framework that ensures the learned policy consistently improves the true reward as the state-action occupancy measure increases. This framework, dubbed Robust Monotonic Policy Learning (RMPL), incorporates a monotonic constraint on the policy's action-values, ensuring that the learned policy does not exploit suboptimal subspaces and thus reduces the risk of reward hacking. RMPL can be combined with other mitigation strategies developed in this paper, such as feature-regularized ORPO and pilot-study-based risk-budgeting, to further improve robustness against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO with and without monotonic constraint, RMPL combined with above mitigation strategies
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RMPL should exhibit improved robustness against reward hacking, ensuring that the learned policy consistently improves the true reward as the state-action occupancy measure increases, while also being scalable to large environments; however, the monotonic constraint may sometimes conflict with other objectives, leading to suboptimal policies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using simulation-to-reality transfer for robust policy evaluation
PROPOSAL: Develop a simulation-to-reality transfer framework for robust policy evaluation. Use a simulation environment to learn a policy that is robust against various scenarios, and then transfer the policy to a real-world environment for evaluation. This framework, dubbed STRPo (Simulation-to-Reality Policy), utilizes a domain adaptation technique to align the simulated and real-world environments, and evaluates the policy's performance in both environments. STRPo can help identify policies that are robust against reward hacking and provide insights into their behavior in different scenarios.
CONTROLS: ORPO with and without simulation-to-reality transfer, STRPo combined with above mitigation strategies
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: STRPo should improve the robustness and generalizability of the learned policies, transferring the knowledge gained from simulation to the real world environment, although the effectiveness of the transfer may depend on the quality of the simulation environment and the alignment between simulated and real-world scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Tighter robust monotonic policy learning for scalable value functions
PROPOSAL: Improve the robust monotonic policy learning framework (RMPL) to obtain a tighter bound on the true reward. This can be achieved by using a more advanced monotonic constraint that leverages the learned policy's occupancy measure. The revised framework, dubbed Tight RMPL, incorporates a novel occupancy-clamping technique that ensures the policy's monotonicity is preserved under the updated constraint. Tight RMPL can be combined with other mitigation strategies, such as feature-regularized ORPO and pilot-study-based risk-budgeting, to further improve robustness against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO with and without monotonic constraint, Tight RMPL combined with above mitigation strategies
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Tight RMPL should improve the robustness and scalability of the learned policies, obtaining a tighter bound on the true reward while reducing the risk of reward hacking; however, the revised monotonic constraint may be more computationally expensive to enforce, and its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the occupancy measure.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Enhanced simulation-to-reality transfer for robust policy evaluation under uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Improve the simulation-to-reality transfer framework (STRPo) to handle uncertainty in the real-world environment. Introduce a novel uncertainty-aware domain adaptation technique that adapts the simulated policy to the real-world environment even when there are differences in the underlying distributions. This revised framework, dubbed STRPo-U, incorporates a probabilistic approach to align the simulated and real-world environments, allowing for more accurate and robust policy evaluation under uncertainty.
CONTROLS: STRPo without and with uncertainty-aware domain adaptation, STRPo-U combined with above mitigation strategies
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: STRPo-U should improve the accuracy and robustness of policy evaluation under uncertainty, allowing for more reliable transfer of knowledge from simulated to real-world environments; however, the effectiveness of the uncertainty-aware domain adaptation technique may depend on the quality of the uncertainty models and the alignment between simulated and real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against varying proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Extend the Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) framework by augmenting it with an ensemble-based approach, where multiple ORPO instances are trained on different proxy rewards drawn from a set of candidate proxies that are assumed to be correlated with the true reward, each with a different correlation level. The base ORPO objective remains the same, but the regularization strength is learned separately for each instance, based on a specified distribution of correlation levels. The ensemble is trained to select the best-performing policy among the instances, which is expected to be robust to varying proxy rewards. Controls will include ablations where a single proxy and correlation level are used, and a baseline using the standard ORPO.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a more robust policy against varying proxy rewards, but its effectiveness may degrade if the correlation levels between proxies are highly uncertain or misspecified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feature-regularized ORPO for improved interpretability
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of ORPO that incorporates feature regularization to improve the interpretability of the learned policy. By promoting policies that have coefficients for certain learned features that are close to those of the reference policy, the features that contribute most to the reward hacking vulnerability can be identified. The regularization term is constructed based on the feature importances of the reference policy, and the coefficients are learned using a combination of standard policy-optimization and standard feature-learning techniques. Controls will include ablations where different feature importance metrics are used and standard ORPO without regularization. The approach is expected to provide insights into how the reference policy exploits certain features, which can inform the design of more robust proxies.
COST: 3240
PREDICTION: This feature-regularized approach should help in identifying which features are most responsible for reward hacking, but it may fail to generalize well when the learned features deviate significantly from those used in the reference policy, or when the reference policy itself is highly complex or overfit.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware ORPO for misspecified correlation levels
PROPOSAL: Modify the ORPO framework to incorporate uncertainty estimation for the correlation level between the proxy reward and the true reward. This can be achieved by modeling the correlation as a random variable with a specified distribution, and incorporating a Bayesian framework to learn a posterior distribution over the correlation level. The regularization strength is then computed based on the estimated posterior distribution. By accounting for the uncertainty in the correlation level, the framework is expected to be more robust to misspecification. Controls will include ablations where a fixed correlation level is used and standard ORPO without uncertainty consideration. The approach is also expected to provide insights into the uncertainty in the correlation estimate.
COST: 4050
PREDICTION: This uncertainty-aware approach should provide a more robust policy when the true correlation level is uncertain or misspecified, but it may suffer from over-conservatism if the uncertainty estimate is overly pessimistic.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a proxy rewards hierarchy via hierarchical RL
PROPOSAL: Address the challenge of proxy reward design by proposing a method that learns a hierarchical structure of proxy rewards. The idea is to frame the problem as a hierarchical reinforcement learning task, where each level of the hierarchy corresponds to a coarser proxy reward. The goal is to learn a policy that optimizes the highest-level proxy reward, while also optimizing lower-level proxy rewards in a way that is consistent with the higher-level objective. This approach is expected to provide a more adaptive and flexible way to learn proxy rewards, especially when the true reward function is complex or uncertain. Controls will include ablations where a single-level proxy reward is used and standard hierarchical RL without a proxy reward hierarchy.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: This hierarchical approach should provide a more flexible and adaptive solution for learning proxy rewards, but it may suffer from exploitation due to local optima in the proxy reward hierarchy and the challenge of balancing higher-level and lower-level objectives.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware ORPO for misspecified correlation levels
PROPOSAL: Revise the uncertainty-aware ORPO framework to incorporate a more principled approach for borrowing robustness information from offline datasets. The idea is to learn an importance-weighted meta-policy that adaptively blends the knowledge from multiple offline datasets with varying proxy reward characteristics, while ensuring that the true reward is still aligned with the proxy reward. This is achieved by learning the importance weights using a set of Auxiliary Task Constraints based on the correlation level uncertainty. By promoting robustness across datasets with varying proxy rewards, the approach aims to improve the robustness and generalization of the policy to unseen scenarios.
COST: 4680
PREDICTION: This revised approach should provide a more robust policy by leveraging information from offline datasets, but it may suffer from domain shift when the datasets are insufficiently diverse or biased, or when the importance weights are overly sensitive to the correlation level uncertainty.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against varying proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Revise the robustifying ORPO approach to incorporate Transfer Learning from a set of pre-trained policies optimized under different proxy rewards and varying correlation levels. By leveraging the pre-trained policies, the framework aims to accelerate the learning process of the target policy under a new or uncertain proxy reward. The transfer of knowledge is facilitated by selecting the pre-trained policy that is most relevant to the target policy, using a metric based on the similarity between the environments or the consequence of each pre-trained policy under the target proxy reward.
COST: 4140
PREDICTION: This transfer-learning augmented approach should accelerate the learning process and improve the robustness of the policy, but it may suffer from over-reliance on the pre-trained policies and potential covariate shift due to the differences between the pre-trained and target scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust proxy reward alignment via deep k-means
PROPOSAL: Develop a method for aligning proxy rewards with the true reward by clustering the state-action space using a deep k-means algorithm. The clusters are adapted to the similarity between the proxy reward and the true reward, such that the proxy reward is maximally "converged" to the true reward within each cluster. The resulting clusters are then used to redefine the state and action spaces, facilitating the optimization of the policy under a more robust and aligned proxy reward. Controls will include ablations where different clustering metrics are used and standard k-means without adaptation to the proxy reward.
COST: 4980
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a robust alignment of the proxy reward with the true reward, but it may fail to generalize well when the clusters are overly sensitive to noise or when the proxy reward diverges significantly from the true reward in certain parts of the state-action space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using simulation-to-reality transfer for robust policy evaluation
PROPOSAL: Apply Simulation-to-Reality Transfer (S2RT) techniques to transfer knowledge from a simulated environment with a well-designed proxy reward to the real-world environment with an uncertain or poorly specified proxy reward. The framework uses a sequence-to-sequence model to learn the mapping between the simulated and real-world states and actions, and then uses this mapping to adapt the policy optimized under the simulated proxy reward to the real-world environment. Controls will include ablations where different transfer learning techniques are used and standard policy evaluation without S2RT.
COST: 5220
PREDICTION: This approach should provide a robust policy evaluation that adapts to the real-world environment, but it may suffer from the limitations of the simulated environment and the potential for simulation error or discrepancies between the simulated and real-world dynamics.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware ORPO for misspecified correlation levels
PROPOSAL: Revise the uncertainty-aware ORPO framework to incorporate a deeper exploration of the decision-making process under uncertainty. The revised approach introduces a Novel Risk-Sensitive Objective that balances the expected value of the policy with the Value-at-Risk of the policy, capturing both the average return and the worst-case return under uncertainty. This allows for more robust policy optimization under uncertain proxy rewards and correlation levels.
COST: 5010
PREDICTION: This revised approach should provide a more robust policy optimization under uncertainty, but it may suffer from increased computational complexity due to the risk-sensitive objective and require careful tuning of the hyperparameters to balance the trade-off between expected value and Value-at-Risk.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Learning a proxy rewards hierarchy via hierarchical RL
PROPOSAL: Revise the learning a proxy rewards hierarchy via hierarchical RL approach to incorporate a Meta-learners framework that adapts to different domains and proxy rewards. The revision introduces a novel Meta-policy that learns to adapt the policy to different environments using a. Minimal learning from experience transfer framework. This allows for a single meta-policy to be adapted to multiple domains and proxy rewards, enabling more efficient and robust learning.
COST: 5880
PREDICTION: This revised approach should provide a more efficient and robust learning of proxy rewards hierarchies, but it may suffer from the challenges of meta-reinforcement learning, such as increased computational complexity and the need for careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the trade-off between adaptability and performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: integrative optimization of rl policies
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel optimization framework that integrates the principles of robust optimization, probabilistic model selection, and regularization to optimize RL policies that are not only robust to the uncertainty in the proxy reward but also aligned with the true reward, leveraging the probabilistic model for principled proxy regression and influence maps for interpretability.

CONTROLS: Evaluate the framework on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, including those from autonomous vehicle traffic control, pandemic response, and blood glucose control; compare the results with traditional metrics such as correlation and regression analysis.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: challenge of proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Reformulate the challenge of proxy rewards as a multi-objective optimization problem, incorporating both the proxy reward and the true reward as separate objectives, and develop a novel algorithm that can efficiently optimize for both objectives simultaneously, using techniques from multi-objective optimization and robust optimization.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the novel algorithm on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, including those from autonomous vehicle traffic control, pandemic response, and blood glucose control; compare the results with traditional RL methods that only optimize for the proxy reward.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the novel algorithm to provide a more comprehensive solution to the challenge of proxy rewards, enabling RL policies that achieve a better balance between the proxy reward and the true reward, and leading to improved robustness and alignment in a range of domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against varying proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Extend the Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) framework by augmenting it with an additional regularization term that upper bounds the maximum absolute difference in true reward between the proxy inconsistent with the ORPO objective and a more trusted proxy, over a certain confidence set of state-action pairs that maximize this difference. Specifically, we propose to minimize a bound on the true loss that is proportional to both the chi-squared divergence between learned and reference policies' state-action occupancy measures and the maximum absolute difference between these two proxies.
CONTROLS: baseline is the standard ORPO algorithm with a fixed proxy, with ablation of each term individually and a combination of both.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (to be confirmed via estimation of the size and complexity of the optimization problem)
PREDICTION: this variant of ORPO is expected to provide better robustness to proxy variations, although the worst-case performance guarantee is limited by the estimation of the maximum absolute difference in true reward over the confidence set of state-action pairs. Failure may occur if the additional term overfits to the training data, or if the upper bound on the true loss is too conservative, leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feature-regularized ORPO for interpretable policies
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of the extended ORPO algorithm from proposal 1 that incorporates feature learning from the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure, and optimizes the policy to have a sparse and interpretable structure. Specifically, we propose to learn a feature vector that aligns with the state-action occupancy measure of the reference policy, and optimize the policy to be a sparse linear combination of these features. This can be achieved through a penalty term added to the optimization objective, e.g., using L1 regularization.
CONTROLS: standard ORPO with and without the feature-learning term, ablation of the L1 regularization.
COST: estimated 30 GPU-hours, as the additional computations required for feature learning and regularization are relatively low compared to the overall optimization process.
PREDICTION: this approach should provide more interpretable policies than standard ORPO, although it may lead to a trade-off between sparsity and reward performance due to the added penalty term. Failure may occur if the learned features do not capture the underlying structure of the reference policy's occupancy measure, or if the L1 regularization is too strong, causing over-simplification of the policy.

TITLE: Uncertainty-aware ORPO for misspecified correlation
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of ORPO that takes into account the uncertainty in the correlation level between the proxy reward and the true reward. Specifically, we propose to model the correlation level as a random variable with a given uncertainty distribution, and update the ORPO objective using a Bayesian approach, incorporating the uncertainty into the optimization process. This can be achieved through the use of variational inference or Monte Carlo dropout.
CONTROLS: standard ORPO and a baseline that assumes a fixed correlation level, with ablation of the uncertainty-aware term.
COST: estimated 75 GPU-hours, as the additional computations required for Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification can be computationally intensive.
PREDICTION: this approach should provide better robustness to misspecified correlation levels, although it may lead to a trade-off between robustness and sample efficiency due to the added computational demands. Failure may occur if the uncertainty model is misspecified, or if the optimization process is slow due to the added uncertainty-aware term.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Iterative Domain Adaptation via Conditional Distribution Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), called Conditional Domain Adaptation (CDA), that iteratively aligns the conditional distributions of the source and target domains, starting from an initial pseudo-labeling step. In each iteration, we match the conditional distributions of a randomly sampled subset of the target data to their source counterparts using a maximum-mean discrepancy (MMD) loss. The source model is then updated based on the pseudo-labeled target data and the MMD loss. We repeat this process until convergence or a predefined number of iterations.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to popular UDA methods, such as Deep Adaptation Networks (DANN), Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN), and MMD-based alignment (MMDA), and to a robust baseline that trains a source-trained model on the worst-case target distribution estimated using a Wasserstein ambiguity set.
COST: 5,376 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our method to outperform state-of-the-art UDA methods on real-world benchmarks for digit recognition and facial attribute classification, but may struggle on tasks with limited unlabeled target data, where sample efficiency and robustness could be more critical.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effective Counterfactual Reasoning for UDA in Scenarios with Limited Target Data
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel counterfactual reasoning approach to address the challenges of UDA when target data is scarce. Our method, called Counterfactual Domain Adaptation (CDA), learns to reason about the counterfactual outcomes of source observations if their features had been drawn from the target domain. Specifically, we use generative models to generate synthetic target features from the source data and train a counterfactual classifier to predict the target labels conditioned on these synthetic features. We then use transfer learning to adapt the counterfactual model to the real target data.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to existing counterfactual-based approaches, such as Bilevel Counterfactual Regret Minimization (BCRM), and ablative experiments to evaluate the importance of various components of our method, including the generative model and the counterfactual classifier.
COST: 9,920 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CDA to outperform state-of-the-art UDA methods in scenarios with limited target data, particularly in tasks that require modeling complex relationships between the source and target domains. However, its effectiveness might be hindered by cases where the source data distribution is vastly different from the target distribution, leading to poor performance in the adaptation step.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Addressing Spurious Correlations via Invariant Risk Minimization for UDA
PROPOSAL: We propose a method called Invariant UDA (I-UDA) that aims to address the issue of spurious correlations in the source data by learning an invariant representation that is independent of the spurious features. I-UDA uses the Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) principle, which involves minimizing the risk under multiple perturbations of the training data. We modify the IRM objective to account for the source and target domain shifts and jointly optimize for the invariant representation and the domain adaptation loss. Our method does not require access to group labels and can learn from limited target data.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to existing UDA approaches that address spurious correlations, such as Causal Deep OnDemand Learning (CDODL) and Domain-Adversarial Style-Transfer networks (DAAT) and evaluate the importance of the modifications to the IRM objective.
COST: 18,750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect I-UDA to demonstrate robustness to spurious correlations and outperform state-of-the-art UDA methods in tasks with source data containing irrelevant features, such as digit recognition and facial attribute classification. However, its effectiveness might be limited in scenarios where the invariant representation is difficult to learn due to the complexity of the domain shifts.

TITLE: robust distributionally robust optimization with counterfactual constraint
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called R-DROCF that combines the ideas of distributionally robust optimization (DRO) and counterfactual fairness (CF) to improve performance in the presence of spurious correlations and distribution shifts. R-DROCF calculates the maximum loss of a predictor under an ambiguity set of possible distributions, with a penalty term added for diverging from a preferred counterfactual distribution representing the ideal data generating process. The counterfactual constraint will remind the model that the label given depends only on the relevant feature for classification when the counterfactual distribution is marginalized over a space of counterfactual labels. The ambiguity set is constructed as a small f-divergence ball around the empirical target distribution to ensure that the robust optimization problem remains computationally tractable.
CONTROLS: compare R-DROCF to group DRO for accuracy in capturing data shifts from source to target data distributions.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: R-DROCF should improve the performance of the model by reducing its reliance on spurious correlations in the source data and ability to generalize to the target domain without group labels, as the counterfactual constraint mitigates data imperfections. When the ambiguity set chosen is too small, significant overfitting may occur due to overly restrictive uncertainty bounds, which fail to account for variability in actual data-generating processes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vanilla Q-Learning with Adaptive Resolution
PROPOSAL: We explore using vanilla Q-learning to select optimal actions in continuous action spaces. The difficulty lies in searching the entire action space to maximize the Q-function. To tackle this, we propose an adaptive resolution approach where we partition the action space into a hierarchical grid and gradually refine the resolution based on our confidence in the current Q-values. Specifically, for a given state, we first sample coarse actions, evaluate the corresponding Q-values, and then refine our search in regions with high Q-values. We estimate Q-values using a neural network with a hybrid architecture combining feedback neural networks and Fourier neural networks.
CONTROLS: Baseline methods include Q-learning with random exploration and a hierarchical actor-critic algorithm.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 1000
PREDICTION: This approach might suffer from locality issues, with the algorithm getting stuck in a local optimum. However, in simpler tasks where local optima are few, it may outperform actor-critic methods, especially in terms of sample efficiency, by propagating knowledge through the hierarchical search.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions as Action Value Refiners
PROPOSAL: Building on the previous proposal, we aim to increase the efficiency of our search by leveraging differentiable conditional compressions. Specifically, we train a neural network to predict the optimal action within a subset of the action space. This prediction network is then used as a refinement of our initial Q-values. We employ differentiable operation strategies such as divergence-based pruning and attention mechanisms to modify the action values dynamically based on the reliability of the current Q-values. This way, we adaptively reduce the dimensionality of our search space, focusing on promising regions.
CONTROLS: The adaptive resolution approach from the previous proposal serves as a control, along with a baseline using uniform random sampling and Q-learning. Additionally, we evaluate our approach in comparison to hierarchical actor-critic algorithms, where the refinement process is coupled with actor training.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 1500
PREDICTION: Expected improvements in terms of sample efficiency and exploration are likely. However, as the differentiable compression operations might introduce a lower level of noise into the Q-function, it might fail in tasks where Q-function locality is mostly due to stochastic variations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions as Action Value Refiners
PROPOSAL: We modify the second proposal by incorporating importance-weighted sampling to downweigh the contributions of actions with low confidence. This allows our approach to focus more on promising regions of the action space while reducing the impact of noisy or uncertain estimates. This modification helps to mitigate the issue of over-reliance on low-probability actions, which can lead to suboptimal performance in certain tasks. We incorporate a probabilistic neural network to learn the action value distribution based on our confidence scores and use this distribution to draw weighted samples during training.
CONTROLS: Our revised proposal will be compared to the original differentiable compression approach as well as the adaptive resolution Q-learning baseline. Additionally, we evaluate our approach in comparison to a baseline using importance-weighted sampling without the adaptive refinement process.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours remains at 1500.
PREDICTION: By effectively downweighting low-confidence actions, our revised approach is likely to achieve better exploration properties and improved action selection performance. However, as the weighted sampling introduces increased variance in the optimization process, it may lead to increased training instability in certain environments.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions as Action Value Refiners
PROPOSAL: We provide a detailed description of the probabilistic neural network used in our revised approach to learn the action value distribution. Specifically, we utilize a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with a neural network-induced prior to predict the parameters of the mixture. The GMM enables our model to efficiently capture multimodal action value distributions and adapt to the underlying structure of the Q-function. PREDICTION: By enabling our model to adapt to complex multimodal action value distributions, the GMM-based prior is likely to improve the accuracy of our action value estimates. However, as the GMM introduces additional parameters, it may suffer from overfitting if not regularized properly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Value-Centered Hierarchical Search (VCHS)
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical search strategy that focuses on exploring the Q-function landscape from a value-centered perspective. Specifically, we first identify a set of promising actions by evaluating a small subset of the action space. Then, we recursively refine the search within the top-performing actions, only considering actions that are likely to lead to higher Q-values. This approach enables us to exploit the structure of the Q-function while avoiding unnecessary exploration of the action space. We implement VCHS using a neural network with a value-encoding layer and a hierarchical action space representation.
CONTROLS: We compare VCHS to our previous proposals, including adaptive resolution Q-learning and differentiable compression with importance-weighted sampling. We also evaluate VCHS against a baseline using uniform random sampling and Q-learning.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 2000
PREDICTION: VCHS is likely to achieve better exploration properties and action selection performance than our previous proposals, especially in environments with sparse rewards or high-dimensional action spaces. However, as the recursive refinement process may lack diversity, it could potentially get stuck in local optima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ensemble of Hierarchical Q-Networks (EHQNs)
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach that combines multiple hierarchical Q-networks to explore the action space, each with a different partitioning of the action space and a distinct search strategy. These networks are trained simultaneously, with the goal of aggregating their predictions to form a comprehensive and robust Q-function estimate. EHQNs enable us to leverage the strengths of different exploration strategies while mitigating their weaknesses. We design EHQNs using a multi-task learning framework, where each Q-network is trained to predict Q-values for a different portion of the action space.
CONTROLS: We compare EHQNs to our previous proposals, including adaptive resolution Q-learning, differentiable compression with importance-weighted sampling, and VCHS. We also evaluate EHQNs against a baseline using ensemble learning without hierarchical search.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 3000
PREDICTION: EHQNs have the potential to outperform our previous proposals by aggregating their strengths and reducing their weaknesses. However, as the model involves multiple Q-networks and complex training dynamics, it may suffer from overfitting or increased training instability if not regularized properly.

ACTION: REVISE

We employ a few-shot learning framework to train the EHQNs ensemble, with the agent-indexed networks being fine-tuned for a few episodes on a new task before making predictions.

COST: Estimated GPU-hours remains at 3000.
PREDICTION: By enabling the ensemble to adapt to new tasks and environments, the meta-learning variant of EHQNs is likely to achieve better out-of-distribution performance and faster task adaptation. However, as the few-shot learning framework may not be robust to optimization instability, it may require careful hyperparameter tuning and regularization to maintain predictive performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scene-Centric Exploration with Grammar-Enriched Lattices
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to exploration in continuous action spaces by leveraging scene-centric grammar-enriched lattices (GELs) to systematically explore the action space. GELs are graph-based representations that capture the structural relationships between actions, allowing for efficient exploration and discovery of optimal actions. We integrate GELs with Q-learning to enable a systematic exploration of the action space, leveraging the intrinsic structure of the environment.
CONTROLS: We compare our GEL-based approach to our previous proposals, including adaptive resolution Q-learning, differentiable compression with importance-weighted sampling, and VCHS. We also evaluate our approach against a baseline using uniform random sampling and Q-learning.

PREDICTION: By leveraging the scene-centric grammar-enriched lattices, our approach is likely to achieve a more systematic and efficient exploration of the action space, discovering optimal actions more quickly. However, as the GELs are learned from data, they may not always capture the underlying structure of the environment correctly, leading to suboptimal performance in certain cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Ratio Estimation for Efficient Value-Based Maximization
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate an optimization method that uses differentiable conditional ratio estimation (DCRE) to approximately maximize the Q-function. Specifically, this approach trains a neural network to estimate the conditional expectation of the Q-function for a given action, then uses gradient-based optimization to maximize the estimated expectation. This method can potentially approximate the value-based maximization without requiring explicit computation of the Q-function gradient.
CONTROLS: The numerically-stable gradient-based approach (Proposal 1) as a baseline. Evaluate on the OpenAI Gym MuJoCo continuous control tasks and the Procgen continuous control benchmark.
COST: 4830
PREDICTION: This approach should be more computationally efficient and scalable than traditional gradient-based methods, but may struggle to accurately estimate the conditional expectation when the Q-function is highly non-linear or when there are multi-modal actions.

TITLE: Investigating Classifier-Free Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: Implement a guided conditional generation variant of the stochastic Kac flow, using classifier-free guidance (a.k.a. noise scheduling), and evaluate its sample quality, diversity, and kinetic energy in unconditional and conditional image generation settings. We will freeze the backbone network trained for unconditional flow and use it as a feature extractor in a smaller, flow-specific discriminator and generator.
CONTROLS: (1) standard classifier-guided adaptation of the backbone network for conditional generation, (2) no guidance during conditional generation, (3) baseline unconditional Kac flow without guidance or adaptation.
COST: 50
PREDICTION: Classifier-free guidance appears to work, enabling the Kac flow to adapt to conditional generation without losing finiteness of kinetic energy, with marginal losses in sample quality and diversity compared to standard classifier-guidance. However, detailed effects on energy metrics and whether optimal noise schedules depend on the specific application and dataset remain to be seen.

TITLE: Analyzing Conditional Energy Bounds for Kac Flows with Guided Sampling
PROPOSAL: Derive a bound on the kinetic energy of the guided Kac flow in conditional image generation, leveraging the fact that the generator's output is aligned with a specific class. Using a sufficiency criterion inspired by planar flows and rotations, we will reason about sufficient conditions under which the guided velocity remains at finite kinetic energy for given guidance and generator architectures.

However, proving sufficiency may be difficult for more complex generator architectures, and we're prepared to see tightness of the derived bounds being somewhat pessimistic.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fast Few-Step Kac Sampler with Preconditoned Gradient Descent
PROPOSAL: Implement a few-step sampler that iteratively refines the reverse-time integral of the Kac flow by preconditioned gradient descent on the signal-noise term. This is inspired by optimization residual methods and adds a stability margin to the basic Kac flow sampling. We will also compare the method with alternative solver strategies, such as Newton's method or sparse preconditioning.
CONTROLS: (1) baseline results for standard unconditional Kac flow sampling, (2) preconditioned gradient descent on a preconditioned residual, without optimization of the preconditioner, and (3) other solvers for comparison, including standard (non-preconditioned) gradient descent.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The preconditioned gradient descent method should improve the sample quality and speed up the sampling process significantly compared to the standard few-step Kac flow, however the degree of improvement might highly depend on the difficulty of the flow, specially if one is very hard to sample or the sampling process is stiff.

PROPOSAL: Modify the global-local-view MLLMs to reduce the number of local crops and induce a balancing effect between the global and local attention streams, making it easier for the model to focus on the most relevant visual tokens. This can be achieved by introducing a novel attention balancing mechanism, where the global attention stream is scaled by the sum of local attention weights, and vice versa.
CONTROLS: Test this mechanism against two baseline models: a standard global-local-view MLLM, and a modified version where the number of local crops is severely decreased to 1.
COST: Estimated compute: 10,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in fine-grained VQA performance, particularly in the presence of distractors and occlusion. This approach might fail if the local crops are too far apart or do not cover all question-relevant regions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention Emphasis Learning (AEL)
PROPOSAL: Design a novel task-agnostic learning objective for the MLLM to focus on question-relevant visual tokens. AEL is a contrastive learning framework where the model is trained to predict a weighted attention distribution over the visual tokens, given the question, such that the weights of question-relevant tokens are emphasized. We will evaluate AEL on multiple real-world datasets, including high-resolution fine-grained visual question answering, and compare its performance with state-of-the-art visual cropping methods like SEAL.
CONTROLS: Compare AEL against a baseline model without AEL, and two ablation studies: 1) training AEL with pseudo-annotations obtained by pseudo-localization algorithms, and 2) using AEL as a late-fusion method with existing global-view MLLMs.
COST: Estimated compute: 50,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We anticipate that AEL will significantly improve the model's ability to focus on question-relevant tokens, resulting in improved fine-grained VQA performance. The main challenge is determining the optimal training procedure for AEL, ensuring that it does not degrade the model's ability to process long-range dependencies.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Attention Emphasis Learning (AEL) with Dynamic Token Importance (DTI)
PROPOSAL: Modify AEL to integrate a dynamic token importance scheme, where the importance of each visual token is adaptively adjusted based on its relevance to the question and the model's predictions. DTI will be implemented as a learned function that scores each token based on its content, position, and prominence in the image. We expect DTI to further improve AEL's ability to focus on question-relevant tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare AEL-DTI against AEL and a baseline model without both, and two ablation studies: 1) evaluating the effect of DTI on the overall performance of AEL, and 2) exploring the use of different token importance metrics.
COST: Estimated compute: 70,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By dynamically adjusting the importance of visual tokens, AEL-DTI is expected to improve the model's fine-grained VQA performance and its ability to handle varying levels of complexity and distractors in the input data. However, there is a risk that DTI may introduce additional error or reinforce existing biases if not implemented carefully.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Visual Attention Driven Local Crops (DVADLC)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new method for local crop generation, where the model itself learns to select and refine the regions of interest (ROIs) relevant to the question. DVADLC uses the output of AEL-DTI to identify the most informative visual tokens and dynamically selects the corresponding ROIs, allowing for adaptive and question-specific local crops. We will compare DVADLC against existing visual cropping methods and evaluate its performance on high-resolution fine-grained visual question answering.
CONTROLS: Compare DVADLC against SEAL, DC², and ViCrop, and two ablation studies: 1) evaluating the effect of the dynamic ROI selection on the overall performance, and 2) exploring the use of different visual token importance metrics in DVADLC.
COST: Estimated compute: 80,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By allowing the model to adaptively select and refine the ROIs, DVADLC is expected to improve the accuracy and efficiency of visual cropping methods on fine-grained VQA tasks. However, there is a risk that the model may select suboptimal regions or overlook important details if not properly fine-tuned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Modal Progressive Aggregation (MMPA)
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel framework that combines the strengths of global-view and global-local-view MLLMs by multi-modal progressive aggregation. MMPA starts with a global view of the image, followed by multiple stages of local crop selection and aggregation. At each stage, the model updates its understanding of the image and question, progressively refining the local crops and aggregating the visual features. We will evaluate MMPA on high-resolution fine-grained visual question answering and compare its performance with state-of-the-art global-local-view MLLMs.
CONTROLS: Compare MMPA against a modified version of global-local-view MLLMs with adaptive local crop selection and two ablation studies: 1) evaluating the effect of the number of stages on the overall performance, and 2) exploring the use of different visual feature aggregation methods in MMPA.
COST: Estimated compute: 100,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: By progressively aggregating visual features from multiple stages, MMPA is expected to improve the accuracy and efficiency of global-local-view MLLMs on fine-grained VQA tasks. However, there is a risk that the model may get stuck in local optima or overlook important details if not properly tuned.

TITLE: A Geometric Alignment Framework with Minimum Camera Motion Assumption
PROPOSAL: We propose a geometric alignment framework that leverages the assumption of minimum camera motion to estimate time offsets between asynchronous videos.
Our method first estimates the camera poses and the 3D structure of the scene using structure-from-motion (SfM) with COLMAP. Then, we apply non-rigid structure-from-motion (NL-SfM) using Colmap to obtain a dense set of 3D feature correspondences across views.
These correspondences are used to compute a geometric cost function that measures the temporal offset between views. The cost function is optimized using a non-convex optimization technique, such as gradient descent with adaptive momentum.
Our approach relies on the assumption of minimum camera motion, which eliminates the need for camera pose tracking and significantly reduces the computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
Controls: We compare our approach to the geometric constraints-based method (proposal 2) and another geometric method, Procrustes analysis for aligning frames.
We also perform ablation studies to evaluate the importance of each component of our framework.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method is expected to achieve state-of-the-art performance on synthetic datasets such as EPFL MultiCam and CrossTown due to its specific assumptions and rigorous optimization process. However, it might not generalize well to real-world datasets with significant camera motion or occlusions.

TITLE: Learning Neuron-Specific Representations from Population Activity
PROPOSAL: Train a graph convolutional network (GCN) on Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice, where each neuron is a node, and edges represent the pairwise temporal correlation between neurons. TITLE: investigating late fusion with modality-specific noise injection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of injecting modality-specific noise into the predictive distributions of a dominant modality on the performance of the weak modality in a decision-level fusion system. Specifically, we will randomly perturb the predictions of the dominant modality with a small amount of noise, designed to match the uncertainty distribution of the weak modality. By doing so, we aim to force the weak modality to adapt to the noisy predictions of the dominant modality, promoting diverse feature utilization and inducing the weak modality to extract more robust and specialized features.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to static late fusion with equal weights, as well as a baseline where the weak modality is trained independently without fusion. To further validate our results, we will also conduct ablation studies on the amount of noise injected at different intensities.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect improved fusion performance and increased robustness for the weak modality, without compromising the dominant modality's accuracy. The potential failure point lies in over-perturbation, where excessive noise injection might destabilize the fusion process or make the weak modality over-sensitive to noise.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Revisit the Linear Read Bottleneck: A Localized Per-Channel Attention Model
PROPOSAL: We propose a localized per-channel attention (LPCA) model, where each channel has a separate memory slot that can retrieve a different past index in each step. LPCA replaces the linear summation in causal softmax attention with a localized token-separable function. We define a learnable per-channel context vector (c_t) for each step t and the input value v_i, and use these vectors to weigh and blend the values in the cache. This way, all steps can still be computed in parallel, and the read can accommodate per-channel, context-dependent selection from memory.
CONTROLS: Standard causal softmax attention (baseline) and ablation without the context vectors.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: LPCA should demonstrate significant relative performance improvements over causal softmax attention on non-sequential tasks like weather forecasting and solar power forecasting, which require per-channel indexing; however, this might fail in highly sequential tasks like electricity transformer load forecasting due to reduced expressivity.

TITLE: Regularization-Based Method for Inter-Modal Catastrophic Forgetting Prevention
PROPOSAL: We propose a regularization-based approach to prevent catastrophic forgetting in UMGMs, called Modal-Aware EWC (MA-EWC). MA-EWC adds a regularization term to the UMGM's loss function that encourages the maintenance of the pre-trained representations for both text and visual modalities. This will be achieved by sharing the weights between the image generation and bitrate estimation tasks, and fine-tuning the model to optimize its performance on both tasks. We will evaluate the trade-off between the accuracy of the bitrate estimation and the quality of the generated images.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline diffusion model that generates images at a fixed bitrate, and experiment with different multi-task learning strategies and fine-tuning schemes to understand their impact on accuracy and image quality.
COST: 50GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach will find a good balance between the accuracy of bitrate estimation and the quality of generated images, and may offer significant benefits in terms of adaptability to changing bitrate constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Experience Quality on RLVR Performance
PROPOSAL: We will create a set of benchmarks using a combination of real-world RLVR datasets from mathematical problem solving, science, and academic exam question answering domains. Each dataset will have a mix of high-quality and low-quality experiences, with the quality of an experience defined by its verifiable reward signal. We will then compare the performance of several state-of-the-art RLVR algorithms, including GRPO, on these datasets, using metrics such as average reward and reasoning accuracy, and analyze the impact of experience quality on their performance.
CONTROLS: GRPO baseline, ablation study to remove high-quality or low-quality experiences from the dataset
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours (10 million interactions across 5 datasets)
PREDICTION: The results will show that high-quality experiences are crucial for the performance of RLVR algorithms, and that neglecting low-quality experiences can lead to suboptimal results. The performance of GRPO may suffer significantly when confronted with datasets containing a high proportion of low-quality experiences.

The goal of this proposal is to establish a systematic understanding of the impact of experience quality on RLVR algorithms, and to provide a baseline for future work.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Efficiency of On-Policy vs. Off-Policy Experiences in RLVR
PROPOSAL: We will extend the previous proposal by incorporating experience replay into the RLVR pipeline. We will modify the GRPO algorithm to incorporate off-policy experiences from a replay buffer, and compare its performance to the on-policy version. Specifically, we will investigate how the efficiency of off-policy experiences, measured by their capacity to improve the model's performance without overwriting existing knowledge, relates to the overall performance of the model.
CONTROLS: On-policy GRPO baseline, ablation study to remove off-policy experiences from the replay buffer
COST: 15,000 GPU-hours (5 million interactions across 5 datasets)
PREDICTION: The results will show that off-policy experiences can significantly improve the efficiency of the RLVR pipeline, particularly when the replay buffer is well-designed, and that the optimal trade-off between on-policy and off-policy experiences is crucial for achieving good performance.

We will also investigate the impact of experience replay on the exploration-exploitation trade-off, and whether off-policy experiences can help alleviate the problem of collapsing the policy into a single trajectory.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Clustering-Based Replay Buffer Management (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We will modify the experience replay mechanism to use a clustering-based approach to manage the replay buffer. This will involve clustering the experiences in the buffer based on their similarity in terms of question and trajectory features. We will then use each cluster as a separate replay buffer, and sample experiences from the buffer according to the importance of the cluster and the novelty of the experience.
CONTROLS: Original on-policy GRPO baseline, modified GRPO algorithm with experience replay, ablation study to remove clustering-based replay buffer
COST: 18,000 GPU-hours (7 million interactions across 5 datasets)
PREDICTION: The results will show that clustering-based replay buffer management can lead to more efficient and effective reuse of past experiences, particularly when the number of clusters is well-tuned, and that this approach can help alleviate the problem of overwriting existing knowledge during experience replay.

This revised proposal aims to address the issue of handling diverse experiences in the replay buffer, and to provide a more principled way of managing the trade-off between exploration and exploitation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Select Relevant Experiences for Replay
PROPOSAL: We will train a neural network to learn the relevance of each experience in the replay buffer to the current policy and question context. The network will take as input the experience, a representation of the current policy and question, and output a relevance score. We will then use this score to select the most relevant experiences for replay, and compare its performance to a random or uniform selection strategy.
CONTROLS: Original on-policy GRPO baseline, modified GRPO algorithm with experience replay and relevance-based selection, ablation study to remove the neural network or the relevance-based selection strategy
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours (8 million interactions across 5 datasets)
PREDICTION: The results will show that learning to select relevant experiences can lead to improved performance and sample efficiency, particularly when the replay buffer contains a large number of experiences with varying relevance.

PROPOSAL: We will develop a novel experience replay method that reweights the experiences in the replay buffer to account for the changing policy during training. This could be computed as the entropy of the implied probability over the relevant space of answer strategies, the norm of the gradient of the change in rewards, or the difference in the agent's understanding of the domain between the start and the end of the trajectory. We measure whether this critique function improves upon traditional objective metrics based on episode terminal rewards, and determine whether using critiqued trajectories for experience replay can stabilize training and accelerate convergence.

TITLE: Optimizing Experience Replay for Large-Scale RLVR
PROPOSAL: We design an end-to-end system that integrates and optimizes the proposed ideas from previous experiments and applies them to large-scale RLVR frameworks. By leveraging efficient data structures and parallel computing, we can accelerate the calculation of trajectory similarity and enable the exploration of larger experience replay buffers. The system is capable of handling various types of data, including question-answer pairs, trajectories, and rewards.
CONTROLS: Baseline GRPO without experience replay optimization, alternative optimization methods based on clustering and retrieval
COST: 16174320
PREDICTION: The proposed system can lead to significant improvements in the sample efficiency, learning speed, and overall performance of RLVR, especially in large-scale reasoning tasks such as math problem solving and science question answering. However, it also requires careful tuning of hyperparameters and optimization of computational resources to achieve the best results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: question difficulty analysis
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to analyze the relationship between question difficulty and the value of a reasoning experience in RLVR. Specifically, we will measure how the difficulty of a question (e.g., measured by human annotators or predicted using a pre-trained difficulty predictor) impacts the reward distribution, trajectory lengths, and the diversity of sampled trajectories. By identifying patterns in these relationships, we aim to develop a theory of question difficulty that informs the selection and weighting of experiences in the replay buffer.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline where question difficulty is not considered, and also analyze the performance of different difficulty predictors on this task.

COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that question difficulty is a strong predictor of reward and trajectory length, and that models performing well on easy questions will struggle with hard ones. However, we may also find that current difficulty predictors are not robust enough to capture the complex relationships between question difficulty and reasoning experience value, which could limit the effectiveness of our approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: entropy-based question filtering
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using entropy-based question filtering to determine which experiences to keep, prioritize and replay in the RLVR optimization process. Specifically, we will implement a variant of our system that only replays experiences from questions with high entropy in the current policy (i.e., questions where the model is uncertain), and compare it to the baseline system that replays experiences uniformly across all questions.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to the baseline system and also analyze the performance of different entropy-based filtering strategies on this task.

COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that entropy-based question filtering improves the sample efficiency and learning stability of the RLVR system, but may lead to a slower initial progress if the model is not given sufficient exploration opportunities. However, if the model's policy is not converged, the exploration-exploitation trade-off might fail if not properly calibrated.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: entropy-based question filtering (revised)
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a revised experiment for entropy-based question filtering. Specifically, we will use a dual-actor critic (DAC) method to adaptively adjust the entropy threshold for filtering questions. The DAC will maintain a policy-specified threshold that automatically increases as the model's policy converges, which may help the model maintain exploration-exploitation trade-off.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to the entropy-based filtering baseline without DAC and also analyze the performance with respect to threshold adjustment parameters.

COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that incorporating DAC in the entropy-based filtering leads to improved convergence speed and stability, but may also increase the risk of getting stuck in local optima if the threshold adjustments are made too aggressively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: trajectory value networks
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of trajectory value networks (TVNs) to evaluate the value of experiences in the replay buffer. Specifically, we will implement a TVN that estimates the value of each stored trajectory based on its ability to lead to successful outcomes when started from different initial states. We will then use these TVN scores to prioritize the replay of most valuable experiences.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uniformly samples from the replay buffer, and also analyze the performance of different TVN architectures on this task.

COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that TVNs improve the efficiency of the RLVR optimization process, but may also lead to overestimation of low-valued trajectories if not properly regularized, and could fail if it is too complex a problem to compute trajectory values precisely.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: policy update mixing
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of policy update mixing to account for the policy mismatch between the stored trajectories and the current policy in the replay buffer. Specifically, we will implement a variant of the RLVR algorithm that mixes the policy update from the stored trajectories with a standard on-policy update, using a proportion that is adjusted based on the TVN scores of the stored trajectories.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uses only standard on-policy updates, and also analyze the performance with respect to different mixing proportions and TVN-based selectors.

COST: 2800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that policy update mixing improves the stability and convergence speed of the RLVR optimization process, but may also lead to slow initial progress if the mixing proportion is too high, and could fail if it is too complex a problem to discern whether the older experiences benefit the relatively current model state.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: trajectory prioritization methods
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to compare different trajectory prioritization methods for experience replay in RLVR. Specifically, we will implement a variety of prioritization methods, including per-traj prioritization, per-step prioritization, and uniform prioritization, and evaluate their performance on the RLVR task. We will also investigate the use of candidate sampling-based prioritization methods.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uniformly samples from the replay buffer, and also analyze the performance of different prioritization methods on different RLVR tasks.

COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that prioritization methods can significantly improve the efficiency of the RLVR optimization process, but may also lead to overestimation of high-priority trajectories if not properly regularized. The prioritization methods may also require careful tuning of hyperparameters, and could behave erratically if the quality of the data within the replay buffer is poor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: model-agnostic experience induction
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of model-agnostic experience induction to generate new experiences that resemble the ones in the replay buffer. Specifically, we will use a combination of importance sampling, diffusion-based forward models, and learned action demonstrations to generate new experiences that are used to augment the replay buffer.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uses only the original experiences in the replay buffer, and also analyze the performance with respect to different model-agnostic induction methods and usage parameters.

COST: 3200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that model-agnostic experience induction improves the diversity and quality of the experiences in the replay buffer, and can lead to more efficient RLVR optimization. However, it may also increase the risk of introducing mode collapse or over-specialization of the model if not properly regularized. The method may require significant computational resources for training, and may fail if the quality of the data within the replay buffer is poor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: failed trajectories re-purposing
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of failed trajectories in the RLVR optimization process. Specifically, we will implement a variant of the RLVR algorithm that re-uses failed trajectories to generate new augmented experiences, and uses these new experiences to augment the replay buffer. We will also investigate the use of re-purposed experience samples to correct distribution mismatch between older and newer policies.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that discards failed trajectories, and also analyze the performance with respect to different re-purposing methods and usage parameters.

COST: 3400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that re-purposing failed trajectories can lead to improved exploration and sample efficiency, but may also lead to increased computation if the number of failed trajectories is high. However, it may also bias the optimization towards sub-optimal solutions if the re-purposing process introduces bugs or irrelevant experiences, which might have to be mitigated via careful selection of model selection or reinforcement algorithms, preferably an efficient exploration-exploration-prediction investigator that allows minimal spending, probing and review per broken routes.

TITLE: self-supervised off-policy dataset collection
PROPOSAL: 
We propose an experiment to investigate the use of self-supervised off-policy dataset collection for experience replay in RLVR. Specifically, we will collect a large dataset of interesting experiences that are collected offline, using a combination of curiosity-driven exploration and self-supervised reward functions, and use this dataset to augment the RLVR optimization process.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uses only online experiences collected during training, and also analyze the performance with respect to different self-supervised reward functions and experience selection methods.

COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that self-supervised off-policy dataset collection can lead to significant improvements in sample efficiency and optimization speed, but may also lead to dataset bias and overestimation of experience value if not properly regularized.

TITLE: grid-based meta-replay

We propose an experiment to investigate the use of grid-based meta-replay for experience replay in RLVR. Specifically, we will organize the experience buffer in a grid structure based on different meta-features (e.g., question difficulty, trajectory value, policy update mix) and use this grid to meta-replay and meta-update the policies in a hierarchical manner, to adapt to changing environments and situations.

CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline system that uses a simple uniform replay and a baseline system that uses global imitation learning methods. We will also analyze the performance with respect to different grid structures and meta-feature combinations.

COST: 3800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that grid-based meta-replay can lead to significant improvements in sample efficiency, convergence speed, and performance on complex tasks, but may also lead to overfitting and increased computational cost if not properly regularized.

TITLE: Graph Invariant Regularizers for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of regularizers for the pre-trained GNN that encourage the network to capture graph invariants that are essential for distinguishing ID and OOD samples. These regularizers modify the pre-trained model by adding a loss function component that aligns with the graph invariant property of triangle preservation, a fundamental property of many real-world graphs. We demonstrate this approach on real-world datasets from social network analysis (e.g., Actor/Actor) and molecular property prediction (e.g., QM9), showing that the modification yields higher OOD scores for OOD samples with respect to ID samples, and lower OOD scores for ID samples with respect to ID samples.

However, it may fail to capture complex OOD distributions with highly divergent structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Tuple Jacobian-Based OOD Detection for Graphs
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of Jacobian-based OOD detection methods for images, we extend this approach to graphs by using multi-tuple Jacobians, which capture higher-order structural relationships within the graph. Our method computes the log determinant of the derivative of the pre-trained GNN's output with respect to the graph's structural features, propagated through multiple convolutional layers. This provides a more detailed and discriminative measure of the graph's internal structure. We use this metric to deliver one-sided probably approximately correct (PAC)-bayes OOD scores for test graphs. We validate this approach on real-world datasets from social network analysis and molecular property prediction.
CONTROLS: Graph Invariant Regularizers for OOD Detection (from Proposal 1), GOODAT
COST: 135000
PREDICTION: This method should provide more informative and robust OOD scores, leveraging the graph's internal structure for detection. However, it may suffer from increased computational cost and may not perform as well on very large graphs due to the expensive computation of multi-tuple Jacobians.

TITLE: Graph Structure Hypothesis Testing for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: In this approach, we reformulate the OOD detection problem as a hypothesis testing problem, where the null hypothesis is that the test graph comes from the ID distribution, and the alternative hypothesis is that the test graph is an OOD sample. We use the pre-trained GNN to extract features from the graph and then apply a statistical test to determine whether the features align with the ID or OOD distribution. The test is based on a graph structure-specific metric, such as the Laplacian spectrum or graph entropy, which encodes the intrinsic structure of the graph. This approach provides a principled and interpretable way to perform OOD detection.

PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training approach that augments the pre-trained GNN with an additional autoencoder module to learn robust representations of graphs in the presence of OOD data. During training, we corrupt the input graphs using a graph neural network-based corruption mechanism, and then use a discriminator to distinguish between the original and corrupted graphs. The pre-trained GNN learns to extract features that are robust to this corruption, effectively learning to detect OOD samples. This approach enables the GNN to learn both a representation of the graph and a confidence measure of the graph's distribution.

PROPOSAL: We analyze the problem of computing and maintaining an empirical Pareto front for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit. We introduce a bound on the cardinality of the Pareto front, and demonstrate that, under certain conditions, this bound can be used to prune the Pareto front, reducing computational costs. Specifically, we show that, with high probability, the Pareto front has at most M*(dim.context^d) arms, where M is a problem-dependent constant and d is the dimensionality of context vectors.

TITLE: Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Linear Bandits
PROPOSAL: We introduce a randomized algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit based on Thompson Sampling. Our algorithm, Multi-Objective Thompson Sampling (MOTS), works by maintaining a collection of samples representing the unknown parameter vectors. At each round, it samples a random reward vector from the resulting posterior distribution, and chooses the arm with the highest sampled reward. We provide a worst-case analysis of the Pareto regret of MOTS, showing that it is sublinear in the number of rounds and scales with the number of objectives L. PROPOSAL: We introduce alternative optimality criteria and regret measures that account for cumulative rewards under repeated selections. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Speculative Decoding for Flow Matching using Draft Rendering
PROPOSAL: Implement a speculative decoding mechanism for FM models by generating multiple drafts in parallel using a lightweight "drafting" network that produces a coarse trajectory, followed by selective verification by the full FM model. The goal is to identify the most promising drafts without excessive full-model evaluations, reducing inference latency without retraining or compromising output quality.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard full-step generation and a basline using a nearest-neighbor search based on the drafts produced by the drafting network.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: We expect a significant reduction in inference latency (35% on average) with negligible reduction in output quality measured using metrics such as Frechet Inception Distance (FID) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), on text-to-image generation and image editing tasks. The approach may, however, fail on tasks requiring high fidelity textures or patterns, due to the coarse granularity of the drafting network.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Drafting Networks for Flow Matching with Guided Trajectory Warping
PROPOSAL: Develop a adversarial training scheme to learn a more effective drafting network by providing it guidance from the full FM model output. Specifically, we introduce a warping loss that encodes the correct endpoint of the draft trajectory (produced by the full model) into the draft's initial conditions, which the drafting network predicts. This encourages the drafting network to produce higher-quality drafts that closely align with the full model's path, thus enabling better speculative decoding.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where the drafting network is trained without the warping loss, as well as a model where the drafting network is pre-trained with a similar loss but without the adversarial supervision from the full model.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: We expect a significant improvement in the quality of drafts produced by the drafting network (-15% improvement in FID score) and -12% improvement in SSIM score, on text-to-image generation, image editing, and text-to-video generation tasks. This might, however, require more extensive fine-tuning, as the warping loss might be brittle and sensitive to model initialization.
