TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Model-Free Online Average Accrual for Static Time Series Forecasts
PROPOSAL: We'll deploy a model-free online averaging algorithm, dubbed online average accrual (OAA), to naively combine the predictions of a pre-trained forecasting model and the previous time step's forecast. OAA adopts the perspective of a statistical analyst, updating a posterior belief over forecasting models conditioned on a sequence of observations. Specifically, at each time step, we maintain a probability distribution over potential forecasting models and update this distribution based on the observations available up to that point. To achieve this, we'll keep track of all previously seen data points and assign each a normalized weight based on their use in the model's prediction, thus creating an effective ensemble that reacts adaptively to distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Average of predictions from pre-trained forecasting models, predictions averaged via a traditional exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) or simple moving average (SMA).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that OAA outperforms traditional approaches to some extent, although high variance of predictions and potential over-reliance on older predictions might hinder its performance when distribution shifts occur frequently and drastically.

TITLE: Adaptive Gradient Estimation through Covariance Matrix Learning with Partial Observations
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the high variance of gradient estimates in online iterations when only a single or a few observations are available, we'll employ a method of learning the covariance matrix of the gradient estimates through partial observations. Our approach will work as follows: at each iteration, we maintain an unbiased estimate of the covariance matrix and use this to imprint an adaptive precision matrix that is injected into the gradient estimator. This precision matrix serves as a regularizer that assessments the quality of our gradient estimates and adapts its weighting based on the magnitude and other characteristics of our partial observations. As time evolves, this learned covariance structure would adjust accordingly, maintaining precise picture of the data.
CONTROLS: A batch of recent samples to construct the empirical covariance matrix, rollout of an ordinary least-squares estimate of the covariance matrix, vanilla online gradient descent without covariance learning.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model should yield more consistent performance even with small-size batches and fewer iterations in more general cases than OGD, though it might incur significant extra cost for learning the covariance matrix and potential overfitting on the variability of partial observations in homogeneous settings.

TITLE: Self-Modifying Online Gradient Descent with Hierarchical Model Updates for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: To tackle online time series forecasting, we propose a self-modifying online gradient descent (SMOGD) algorithm, which updates the model parameters based on the latest arrival data and adaptively adjusts the learning rate to account for the changing distribution of the data. Additionally, we propose a hierarchical model update scheme, where the model updates are performed in a two-stage process: the initial update is performed using the standard gradient descent, and the subsequent updates are performed using a modified gradient descent with adaptively learned parameters, enabling efficient adaptation to concept drift in the data.
CONTROLS: SMOGD with fixed learning rate, standard online gradient descent (OGD), SMOGD without hierarchical update stage.

PREDICTION: SMOGD is expected to outperform traditional online time series forecasting methods by adaptively adjusting the learning rate and model parameters to the changing distribution of the data, leading to improved forecasting accuracy.

PROPOSAL: To detect concept drift in time series data before it significantly impacts the forecasting performance, we propose a novel early warning system based on statistical process control (SPC) and cumulative sum (CUSUM) methods. CONTROLS: Traditional drift detection methods, such as one-class SVM and data stream-based approaches.

PREDICTION: Our proposed early warning system is expected to provide a significant improvement in detecting concept drift in time series data, allowing for more timely and effective model updates to maintain accurate forecasting performance.

PROPOSAL: We propose an extension to online gradient descent (OGD) that allows for the adaptation of the loss function during training, enabling the algorithm to adjust to drift in the data distribution. Our approach introduces self-modifying loss functions that modify their weights to prioritize recent samples more strongly when drift is detected, promoting more accurate predictions under changing conditions. We will experimentally evaluate its performance on challenging real-world time series forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare with OGD, adaptive loss functions, and drift-detection-based methods that adjust the loss function.
COST: 1581
PREDICTION: Our self-modifying OGD is expected to outperform traditional OGD under various drift scenarios, particularly when large distribution shifts occur, but may require additional tuning to optimize performance across different tasks and drift patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Early Warning System for Concept Drift in Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We develop an early warning system that detects concept drift in time series forecasting using a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques. Our system identifies drift before it significantly affects the model's performance, enabling timely adjustments to prevent suboptimal forecasts. We will evaluate its performance on a range of real-world datasets and assess its ability to reduce the impact of drift on forecasting accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing drift-detection methods and OGD variants that select update strategies based on known drift patterns.
COST: 1429
PREDICTION: Our early warning system is expected to provide reliable drift detection and significantly reduce the impact of drift on forecasting accuracy, particularly in environments where drift is frequent or severe, but may require additional tuning to optimize performance across different tasks and drift patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferring Adaptation Knowledge for Cross-Dataset Concept Drift
PROPOSAL: We propose a framework for transferring adaptation knowledge between time series forecasting tasks with different datasets, enabling better adaptation to concept drift in scenarios where previously learned adaptations can be leveraged. Our method uses meta-learning to distill adaptation knowledge from a set of source tasks and applies it to target tasks, accelerating the adaptation process and improving forecasting accuracy. We will experimentally evaluate its performance on multiple real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with non-transferring adaptation methods, OGD, and meta-learning approaches that adapt to each new task separately.
COST: 1699
PREDICTION: Our adaptation transfer method is expected to effectively leverage knowledge from source tasks to improve adaptation to new tasks, particularly when source and target tasks share similar drift patterns or characteristics, but may require additional tuning to balance transfer and task-specific adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: parameter adaptation in online time series forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of five adapter-based methods: (1) updating final-layer weights, (2) updating input weights, (3) updating output weights, (4) updating the entire adapters (typically 1-2 MLPs), and (5) updating only the output layer of the adapters. We will experiment with three real-world datasets: traffic flow forecasting (M5 forecast), electricity consumption forecasting (M4 competition), and solar power forecasting (IEEE dataset). The methods will be compared using mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) as the evaluation metric.

PREDICTION: We expect adapter-based methods to outperform OGD on the traffic flow and solar power datasets, and it's possible that OGD could perform better on the electricity consumption dataset due to its complexity.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Reformulating Pseudo-Label Encoding for Enhanced Robustness
PROPOSAL: Examine the effectiveness of a soft pseudo-label encoding, where instead of using a one-hot representation, classes are represented by a soft vector with a Gaussian distribution centered at the predicted class. This is achieved by smoothly distributing the class probabilities across neighboring classes, incorporating information about the uncertainty of the prediction.
CONTROLS: Evaluate this approach against two ablations: (1) a "filtered" pseudo-label encoding, where the top K predicted classes are kept, and (2) a "focal" pseudo-label encoding, where the noise is reduced by concentrating on hard classes and down-weighting easy ones.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Soft pseudo-label encoding is expected to provide a good balance between low label noise and low mislabeling rates. This encoding form could fail when dealing with very sparse or separated class distributions, where it might not capture the correct class identity effectively.

COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Introducing class-dependent perturbations could enhance the robustness of pseudo-label learning by exploiting the differences in class ambiguity and confidence, leading to improved accuracy in segmentation tasks. However, it may also increase the risk of overfitting if not carefully tuned.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Deep ReLU Networks Have a Polynomial Dependence on the Data Size for the Single Neuron Case
PROPOSAL:  In the infinite-width limit, and assuming that the training data is NTK-separable with a margin of $\gamma$, we prove that a single ReLU neuron trained with GD converges to a solution that generalizes to any test data with a risk bound of order $\mathcal{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$. This is done by analyzing the NTK of a single ReLU neuron and showing that it can be inverted with a condition number bounded polynomially in $n$ and $\gamma$.
CONTROLS:  Vanilla GD, fixed learning rate, GD with a small single-layer pre-training to show the upper-bound is tight.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (only the inversion of the NTK Gram matrix is computationally expensive).
PREDICTION:  This result should be achievable, given that we only need to prove a polynomial dependence of the NTK's condition number on the data size, a relatively more tractable task than dealing with a full neural network. The tightness of the upper-bound is sensitive to the choice of the single-layer pre-training.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: High-Probability Convergence Guarantees for Deep ReLU Neural Tangent Kernels with Finite Width
PROPOSAL:  For $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, we establish a high-probability convergence guarantee for the NTK linearization of a deep ReLU network with $L$ layers and finite width $m$. Specifically, for data separated by the NTK features with a margin $\gamma$, we prove that with high probability, the GD trajectory converges to a solution that has a generalization error bounded by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{L\log m / (\gamma^2 n \epsilon)})$.
CONTROLS:  Previous result 1 with a finite width $m$, small single-layer pre-training, and an additional noise term that represents the high-probability convergence guarantee.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (the calculation involves several intricate analyses of the NTK Gram matrix).
PREDICTION:  This high-probability convergence guarantee for the NTK linearization of a deep ReLU network might be slightly suboptimal depending on the constant beneath the logarithm, which we did not carefully calibrate in our parameter choices.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Bounds on the Minimum Eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel Gram Matrix for ReLU Networks
PROPOSAL:  We study the NTK Gram matrix $\mathbf{H}^\infty$ of a deep ReLU network and derive a lower bound on its minimum eigenvalue. Specifically, we show that for a network of width $m$, $\lambda_0(\mathbf{H}^\infty) \geq \Omega(\min\{1/m, 1/L\})$, where $L$ is the number of layers in the network. This lower bound holds for any ReLU activation and any initialization scheme.
CONTROLS:  Upper bounds on the minimum eigenvalue from previous results, various activation functions, and initialization schemes.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (only requires matrix manipulations and eigenvalue calculations).
PREDICTION:  We anticipate that the lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue will be tight, meaning that the previously obtained upper bounds on the minimum eigenvalue are indeed optimal. This result can improve our understanding of the NTK Gram matrix and shed more light on its properties.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improved Bounds on the Minimum Eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel Gram Matrix for ReLU Networks
PROPOSAL:  We refine the lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the NTK Gram matrix for a deep ReLU network, and show that $\lambda_0(\mathbf{H}^\infty) \geq \Omega(1/(m\sqrt{L}))$. This improved bound depends on both the network width $m$ and the number of layers $L$. We achieve this improvement by analyzing the effect of the ReLU activation on the NTK Gram matrix.
CONTROLS:  The same controls as before, along with the updated result from the refinement.
COST:  No additional compute is required, as the revision only changes the statement of the result and its analysis.
PREDICTION:  Our refinement should improve the understanding of the NTK Gram matrix and its properties. This result can have implications for the derivation of convergence rates for deep ReLU networks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Polynomial Width Requirements for Deep ReLU Networks with Optimistic Rademacher Complexity Bounds
PROPOSAL:  We derive optimistic Rademacher complexity bounds for ReLU networks that achieve an upper bound of the form $\mathcal{O}(1/n\gamma^2)$ for the risk of the network. These bounds imply that a polynomial width $m = \mathrm{poly}(L,n,1/\gamma)$ is sufficient for a deep ReLU network to achieve this upper bound. We also derive an improved margin lower bound $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/L)$ that indicates the effect of depth on margin.
CONTROLS:  The previous result on the high-probability convergence guarantee, and the theoretical minimax rate for binary classification.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (requires calculations involving the NTK Gram matrix and Rademacher complexity).
PREDICTION:  This result might be slightly suboptimal due to the pessimistic choice of activation functions excluded from the proof. However, we anticipate that the requirement for a polynomial width would generally be necessary for the deep ReLU network.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Low-Regret Guarantees for Gradient Descent on Separable Deep ReLU Networks with Non-Zero Margin
PROPOSAL:  We establish a low-regret guarantee for GD on a deep ReLU network with non-zero margin. Specifically, we show that for a gradient-descent training sequence of length $T$, the averaged test error can be upper bounded by $\mathcal{O}(1/(\gamma^2 n))$ when $T$ exceeds certain threshold $T(\gamma,n)$. Furthermore, for sufficiently large depth, this upper bound can be related to the theoretical minimax rate for binary classification.
CONTROLS:  Previous result on optimistic Rademacher complexity bounds, and existing low-regret guarantees for GD on certain types of neural networks.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (requires intricate asymptotic analysis and careful bound derivations).
PREDICTION:  Although the low-regret guarantee seems promising, the derived upper bound might not match the theoretical minimax rate due to incorporation of a sufficient learning steps limitation.

ACTION: ADD 6

TITLE: estimating epistemic uncertainty with masked diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate whether masked diffusion models (MDMs) can serve as a strong alternative for estimating epistemic uncertainty, despite their well-documented efficacy in language modeling. We'll pre-train an MDM on a standard language modeling task, and then fine-tune it on a semi-supervised task where the input is paired with the target and noisy versions of the input, both generated by the model itself. This will allow the model to learn the structure of the input-output pairs, including the boundaries between the inputs and the outputs. We'll then treat the semi-supervised model as an explicit probabilistic model and estimate the epistemic uncertainty by sampling from it, by counting the proportion of possible future inputs that can generate the same output sequence.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our results with existing methods for estimating epistemic uncertainty in fully-supervised settings and ablate the semi-supervised fine-tuning step to see its contribution. We'll also compare the results of our pre-trained MDM to those of a pre-trained autoregressive model (T5) with the same level of parameters, to see whether the masked diffusion model performs any better or worse in this task.
COST: 280 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect our MDM-based method to outperform existing methods for estimating epistemic uncertainty in fully-supervised settings, but might struggle to model long-range dependencies and predictions beyond the scope of the semi-supervised training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against varying proxy rewards
PROPOSAL: Extend the Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) framework by augmenting it with an ensemble-based approach, where multiple ORPO instances are trained on different proxy rewards drawn from a set of candidate proxies with varying assumed correlations. At inference time, the policy that achieves the highest true reward under a maximum likelihood estimate of the true reward is chosen. This approach leverages the diversity of proxy rewards to identify a policy that performs well across a range of possible true rewards.
CONTROLS: (1) Ablation study of individual ORPO instances with varying correlation levels, (2) comparison with a baseline that trains a single ORPO instance with the average correlation level and multiple successful proxy rewards, and (3) ORPO without the ensemble-based approach as a separate baseline.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should provide improved robustness to varying proxy rewards, but its additional computational cost might lead to overfitting on the synthetic data, necessitating further experiments with more realistic scenarios or smaller datasets to demonstrate its efficacy in real-world settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Feature-regularized ORPO for improved interpretability
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of ORPO that incorporates feature regularization to improve the interpretability of the learned policy. By promoting policies that have coefficients for certain learned features that are close to those of the reference policy, the features used by the policy can be made more transparent and explainable. This variant is dubbed Feature-Regularized Occupational Policy Optimization (FORPO).
CONTROLS: (1) Ablation study of feature regularization strength, (2) comparison with standard ORPO and a baseline that uses feature importance analysis on the policy, and (3) human evaluation of the interpretability of policies learned with different regularization strengths.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: FORPO is likely to improve the interpretability of the learned policy, but the choice of features may require manual tuning or may be dominated by proxy reward correlations. Its integration with the ensemble-based approach from Prop 1 could provide further insights into the robustness of the reference policy's state-action features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-aware ORPO for misspecified correlation levels
PROPOSAL: Modify the ORPO framework to incorporate uncertainty estimation for the correlation level between the proxy reward and the true reward. This can be achieved by modeling the correlation as a random variable with a prior distribution, and incorporating a Bayesian update based on the observed state-action pairs. The policy optimization objective is then modified to account for the estimated uncertainty, allowing the policy to adapt to misspecified correlation levels.
CONTROLS: (1) Ablation study of prior distribution choices and update frequency, (2) comparison with standard ORPO and a baseline that uses a fixed, assumed correlation level, and (3) evaluation on synthetic datasets where the true correlation level is varied.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification should provide improved robustness to misspecified correlation levels, but its effectiveness may depend on the quality of the prior distribution and the update frequency, which may require tuning. It is likely to be most effective when combined with the ensemble-based approach from Prop 1.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling-based exploration for unvisited state-action pairs
PROPOSAL: Adapt the exploration strategy in ORPO to prioritize sampling state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits. This can be achieved by using a biased sampling distribution that preferentially selects state-action pairs with low reference policy occupancy. By increasing the sampling frequency in these regions, the policy can learn more about the true reward in areas where the correlation constraint has little information.
CONTROLS: (1) Comparison with standard ORPO and a baseline that uses a uniform sampling distribution, (2) evaluation of policy performance on synthetic datasets with wide state-action visitation distributions, and (3) analysis of the effect of exploration bias on the learned policy values.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This modification should improve the policy's performance in regions with low reference policy occupancy, but it may lead to overexploration in these areas if not properly calibrated.

CONTROLS: Use the same datasets as in Relative Entropy Based Guidance for Diffusion Models to evaluate the time evolution of the intermediate distributions, and compare the results with the performance of the guidance mechanisms.

CONTROLS: Compare the proposed method to the baseline methods, Scaling and Regularization for Robust Inference, and evaluate its ability to maintain manifold feasibility and explore the solution space on phase retrieval and high dynamic range (HDR) image reconstruction datasets from the experimental domains.

CONTROLS: Compare the proposed method to the baseline methods and evaluate its ability to maintain manifold feasibility and explore the solution space on image super-resolution, image inpainting, and image deblurring datasets from the experimental domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Alignment-Based Methods to Spurious Correlations
PROPOSAL: We will use a real-world dataset (e.g., FMNIST or CIFAR-10-C) with label noise introduced through spurious correlations between input features and labels. We will train and compare the performance of state-of-the-art alignment-based UDA methods (e.g., Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks, CORAL) on the noisy source data and their ability to adapt to the clean target data. We will use metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. Our controls will include the performance of the methods on clean data and the effect of different levels of label noise.
CONTROLS: Same UDA methods on clean data, ERM on clean source data, influence of different levels of label noise
COST: 20 GPU-hours

Pseudo-labeling may perform better in some scenarios due to its self-training nature, which can help to gradually learn to ignore noisy labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Symmetry-Based Graph Convolutions for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Design a graph neural network (GNN) architecture that incorporates symmetry-based graph convolutions (SBC) to learn the operator structure of PDEs. We propose to extend the physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework by introducing SBCs that preserve the underlying symmetries of the PDEs, such as rotational and translational invariances. We will utilize the graph convolutional layers to learn the spatial patterns and evolution of the PDE solutions, and the SBCs to enforce the physical constraints and symmetries. The architecture will be trained on a set of synthetic PDE datasets with varying source terms and geometries.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard PINNs and graph-based solvers (e.g., Physics-Informed Graph Convolutional Networks (PI-GCN)).

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporal graph attention mechanism (TGAT) to capture the dynamics of source terms over time. This will enable the model to generalize to unseen source term trajectories and improve its adaptation to time-varying external forcing. We will train the model on a range of synthetic PDE datasets with varying source term dynamics and geometries.
CONTROLS: Comparison to models without TGAT (i.e., SBC-GNN from proposal 1) and to standard PINNs using additional source term history as input.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (expanding existing architecture and exploration of hyperparameters).
PREDICTION: The addition of TGAT will improve the model's generalization to unseen source term dynamics, but may increase the risk of overfitting to the training trajectories.

This revised architecture will be tested on a range of synthetic PDE datasets with varying source term geometries and intensities.

We will test the IGN on a range of synthetic and simulated PDE datasets from reaction-diffusion dynamics, including phase separation, population dynamics, and excitable media.

PROPOSAL: Develop a neural operator that learns to preserve the conservation laws of PDEs, such as mass conservation in contaminant transport and momentum conservation in fluid dynamics. We will design a neural network that takes into account the underlying physical constraints and learns to propagate the solution using a conservation law-invariant operator. This will be tested on a range of synthetic PDE datasets from contaminant transport and fluid dynamics.
CONTROLS: Comparison to the REVISED SBC-GNN (proposal 1), Invariant Graph Network (proposal 3), and standard PINNs on contaminant transport and fluid dynamics datasets.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of domain-invariant features to enable transfer learning across PDE domains. This will be tested on a range of synthetic PDE datasets from various domains, including reaction-diffusion dynamics, contaminant transport, and fluid dynamics.
CONTROLS: Comparison to pre-training the neural networks on a single PDE domain and fine-tuning on other domains, and to standard PINNs on each PDE domain separately.

This will be tested on synthetic PDE datasets with large-scale geometries and complex PDEs.
CONTROLS: Comparison to the REVISED SBC-GNN (proposal 1), Invariant Graph Network (proposal 3), and standard PINNs on large-scale geometries and complex PDEs.

PROPOSAL: Explore the use of meta-learning to enable few-shot learning for PDEs. We will design a meta-learning framework that trains a model to learn the solution to a PDE on a small number of examples and then adapts to new, unseen PDEs with few additional training samples. This will be tested on a range of synthetic PDE datasets from various domains.
CONTROLS: Comparison to standard PINNs and the other proposals in the set, and to few-shot learning approaches without meta-learning.
COST: 2800 GPU-hours (design and training of meta-learning framework).
PREDICTION: The meta-learning framework will enable few-shot learning for PDEs, allowing the model to adapt to new, unseen PDEs with few additional training samples. However, the performance may degrade if the new PDEs are significantly different from the ones seen during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty Quantification for Neural PDE Solvers
PROPOSAL: Develop a framework for uncertainty quantification for neural PDE solvers, which will enable the estimation of the uncertainty associated with the solution of a PDE using a neural network. We will use techniques such as Monte Carlo dropout and Bayesian neural networks to quantify the uncertainty in the solution. This will be tested on a range of synthetic PDE datasets from various domains.
CONTROLS: Comparison to other proposals in the set and to standard methods for uncertainty quantification in neural networks.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (design and training of uncertainty quantification framework).
PREDICTION: The framework will enable accurate uncertainty quantification for neural PDE solvers, which is essential for applications where the solution accuracy matters. However, the computational cost may be high due to the need for multiple forward passes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Convergence of Vision-Language Alignments for Generalization
PROPOSAL: We investigate how the alignment of visual and text features in CLIP-based methods contributes to zero-shot HOI detection generalization. We propose modifying the standard CLIP alignment loss to incorporate an information-theoretic term that encourages the aligned features to capture fine-grained semantic information from interaction descriptions.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard CLIP alignment, ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the proposed term.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Modifying the alignment loss results in improved generalization to unseen interactions, but may introduce overfitting to the fine-grained noise in the interaction descriptions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Object-Agnostic Interaction Recognition with Dynamic Visual Hierarchy
PROPOSAL: We propose an object-agnostic architecture that dynamically constructs a visual hierarchy of human-object interactions using a transformer-based graph neural network. This approach allows the model to automatically focus on interactions relevant to the image and ignore irrelevant ones, without relying on a specific object detector. The visual hierarchy is trained to explain the output of the interaction classifier, which is composed of a set of learned attention filters that query the input image for relevant interaction features.
CONTROLS: Comparison with existing two-stage methods that couple interaction recognition with a specific object detector, an ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the dynamic visual hierarchy.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Object-agnostic interaction recognition shows significant improvement over existing two-stage methods, but may suffer from reduced performance on images with complex scenes or difficult humanObjectContext detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Convergence of Vision-Language Alignments for Generalization
PROPOSAL: We refine the initial proposal by introducing a new tokenizer-based method that jointly learns to align visual and text features using a common token space. This approach allows for more efficient and flexible alignment of visual and text features, and can be used in conjunction with the modified alignment loss proposed earlier. Additionally, we propose to use a contrastive loss function to further improve the alignment.
CONTROLS: Comparison with the original standard CLIP alignment, ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the tokenizer-based alignment and contrastive loss.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Tokenizer-based alignment with contrastive loss outperforms the original standard CLIP alignment, but may still suffer from limited generalization to very unfamiliar interaction types due to the complexity of the visual features.

TITLE: Evaluating the Importance of Human-Object Relevance for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough analysis of the importance of human-object relevance for zero-shot HOI detection. We adopt a data split methodology that separates images into relevant and irrelevant classes based on the objects that appear in the scene and the actions that are being performed. We then train models on these datasets and evaluate their accuracy on a series of benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard zero-shot HOI detection benchmarks, evaluation using a range of object-centred metrics.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Evaluating the importance of human-object relevance reveals that models are significantly more accurate on images where the objects are relevant to the actions being performed, but may struggle with images where the objects are not relevant.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Few-Shot Adaptation for Zero-Shot HOI Detection
PROPOSAL: We investigate the feasibility of using a few-shot adaptation mechanism to fine-tune our models for zero-shot HOI detection. We explore different adaptation strategies, including online meta-learning and offline meta-learning, and evaluate their effectiveness in improving performance on novel interactions. We also study the effect of different adaptation settings, such as few-shot training datasets and adaptation iterations.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard zero-shot HOI detection models, evaluation using a range of meta-learning metrics.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Few-shot adaptation shows significant improvement over standard zero-shot HOI detection models, but may require a large number of adaptation iterations to converge.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Object-Agnostic Interaction Recognition with Dynamic Visual Hierarchy
PROPOSAL: We refine the dynamic visual hierarchy proposal by incorporating a novel graph attention mechanism that adaptively selects the attention weights based on the hierarchy of interactions. This allows the model to focus on the most relevant interactions in the image, rather than spreading its attention across all possible interactions. We also propose a new loss function that encourages the model to capture multiple interactions per human-object pair.
CONTROLS: Comparison with the original object-agnostic interaction recognition model, ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the graph attention mechanism and new loss function.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised object-agnostic interaction recognition model shows significant improvement over the original model, with improved accuracy and robustness to complex scenes and imperfect humanObjectContext detection.

TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Zero-Shot HOI Detection with Likelihood Weighting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel likelihood weighting scheme to quantify the uncertainty associated with the predicted interactions. We use an ensemble of models to generate multiple hypotheses for each human-object pair, and then compute the likelihood of each hypothesis based on the confusion matrix of the models. We then use this likelihood weighting to compute a final interaction probability that takes into account the uncertainty of the predictions.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard zero-shot HOI detection models, evaluation using a range of uncertainty-aware metrics.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Uncertainty-aware zero-shot HOI detection shows significant improvement over standard models, with improved robustness to noisy and uncertain inputs.

We propose a novel label splitting strategy that balances the distribution of interaction labels among the models.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard multi-label zero-shot HOI detection models, evaluation using a range of multi-label metrics.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Composed models show significant improvement over standard models, with improved coverage and accuracy for multi-label zero-shot HOI detection.

PROPOSAL: We leverage video knowledge to enhance zero-shot HOI detection by incorporating action-verb and object-verb relations into the model. CONTROLS: Comparison with standard zero-shot HOI detection models, evaluation using a range of human-centric metrics.

PREDICTION: Human-centric zero-shot HOI detection with video knowledge shows significant improvement over standard models, with improved robustness to various environmental settings and improved understanding of human behavior.

PROPOSAL: We propose a unified framework that integrates the key components from our previous proposals to achieve state-of-the-art performance for zero-shot HOI detection across various domains and scales. Our framework leverages a dynamic visual hierarchy, few-shot adaptation, uncertainty-aware estimation, and human-centric video knowledge to detect accurate and robust human-object interactions.
CONTROLS: Comparison with standard zero-shot HOI detection models, evaluation using a range of domain-agnostic and scale-agnostic metrics.
COST: 8000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework achieves significant improvement over standard models, with improved robustness to domain shifts and scale variations, and state-of-the-art performance on various zero-shot HOI detection benchmarks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-Exemplar Few-Shot Refinement for Conditional Image Generators
PROPOSAL: We design and evaluate a novel few-shot refinement method, dubbed Real-Exemplar Fine-Tuning (REF), which adapts the quality and diversity of off-the-shelf conditional generators using only a small number of real exemplar images, without fine-tuning the generator. This approach leverages a neural network to approximate the rate of change in Q-values, allowing for efficient exploration of the action space.

TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions as Action Value Approximators
PROPOSAL: We propose differentiable conditional compressions (DCCs) as a novel approach to approximate the action value function without discretizing the action space. DCCs learn to compactly represent a family of action-value functions, each acting as an intermediate compression of the original Q-function, and use these compact representations to approximate the value of unseen actions. This method allows us to compute the optimal action without arguing with the advantage function directly.
CONTROLS: We compare our DCC to a neural network-based Q-function approximator, evaluating both on the expected accuracy of their action predictions and the neural network's learnability
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our DCC approach will demonstrate improved accuracy in action prediction and faster learning rates compared to a neural network-based Q-function approximator, but may struggle when encoding complex multi-modal Q-functions, and exhibit a larger memory footprint due to the need to maintain multiple compressed representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Attention Warm-Up for Local Cropping
PROPOSAL: To alleviate the issue of the MLLM struggling to identify the few visual tokens that are relevant to the question from the large number of local crop tokens, we modify the local cropping strategy to include a cross-attention warm-up. Specifically, we insert a layer that queries the entire image's representation with the question embedding and then uses the resulting attention weights to sample a subset of local crops that are most relevant to the question, and use these crops as the input to the MLLM.
CONTROLS: Compare this warm-up strategy to a standard local cropping strategy without cross-attention, and also compare to models with a hierarchical search-based approach like DC². This will help us understand whether the introduction of cross-attention can already provide significant benefits.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (linear scaling to 5000 local crops)
PREDICTION: This method should significantly outperform standard local cropping and approach the results of DC², though it might still struggle with images containing many distractors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention Emphasis Learning for Visual Cropping
PROPOSAL: Another challenge faced by existing visual cropping techniques is the difficulty in defining a suitable question-guided heatmap that captures the relevance of each image region. To address this, we introduce a novel attention emphasis learning technique that allows the MLLM to learn to emphasize the most relevant regions in the image based on the question. We achieve this by adding an extra classification head to the MLLM that rates the importance of each region, and then use this importance score to compute a weighted average of the region embeddings.
CONTROLS: Compare this attention emphasis learning technique to ViCrop, and also compare to a variant of ViCrop that uses the MLLM's standard self-attention mechanism to compute the heatmap. This will help us understand whether the emphasis learning can improve heatmap computation and guide more effective visual cropping.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may offer improvements over ViCrop and comparable performance to using the standard self-attention mechanism in ViCrop.

We achieve this by concatenating the output of the cross-attention warm-up with the image embedding and using the concatenated vector as the input to the importance scoring head.

TITLE: Dynamic Region Graph Construction
PROPOSAL: To address the scalability issue of exhaustive hierarchical search methods like DC² and to make the attention emphasis learning more effective, we propose a novel dynamic region graph construction method. This method constructs a graph where nodes represent image regions, and edges represent associations between regions. The graph is dynamically constructed on-the-fly during inference based on the question and the image features, allowing the model to selectively focus on the most relevant regions without exhaustive search. We then use this graph to weight the importance of each region in attention emphasis learning.
CONTROLS: Compare this dynamic region graph construction method to hierarchical search methods like DC² and also compare to attention emphasis learning with static region graphs.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (mainly due to the construction of the dynamic region graph during inference)
PREDICTION: This method can effectively prune unnecessary regions and may offer significant performance improvements over hierarchical search methods, while providing a more efficient alternative to exhaustive search.

RPAG can adaptively focus on the most relevant regions, integrating the strengths of both cross-attention warm-up and attention emphasis learning while avoiding the weaknesses of a fixed importance scoring.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Zero-Variance Prompts with Group Reward Normalization
PROPOSAL: This experiment emulates Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) but replaces the group reward normalization with a novel approach where each response's reward is normalized within the batch rather than the group. We will also include two controls: (1) standard GRPO with original group reward normalization and (2) a naive version of GRPO where each response's advantage is computed independently without normalization. The batch-normalized variant will be implemented in a batch that contains a mix of prompts of varying variance and in a batch that contains solely zero-variance prompts.
CONTROLS: Standard GRPO, naive GRPO (independent computation of advantages), and filtering zero-variance prompts out before rollout
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Batch-normalized GRPO is expected to outperform standard GRPO when prompted with zero-variance prompts, but may fail when encountering mixed batches or batches with very large variance, as it may become unstable due to the dominance of a single group undergoing normalization.

Turn 1's novel approach addresses the central issue of zero-variance prompts by attempting to find a different way to normalize the advantages, thereby still exploiting rollouts with identical rewards.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Harnessing Zero-Variance Prompts for Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether exploiting zero-variance prompts for multi-task learning can lead to improved overall performance and more stable training. The experiment will use a hierarchical policy architecture, where a top-level policy determines the task and a bottom-level policy is trained to perform the task. We will include five controls: (1) standard multi-task learning without exploiting zero-variance prompts, (2) using GRPO with filtering of zero-variance prompts, (3) standard multi-task learning with batch-normalized GRPO (proposed in Turn 1), (4) using GRPO with the novel prompt classification approach (which predicts which prompts are likely to yield identical rewards and skips them), and (5) using DAPO (Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization) for comparison.
CONTROLS: Standard multi-task learning, GRPO with filtering, batch-normalized GRPO, GRPO with novel prompt classification, DAPO
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment may find that multi-task learning with zero-variance prompts leads to improved overall performance on tasks that receive significant training signal from these prompts. However, it may fail when mixed tasks are present, as it may cause instabilities in the training process due to inconsistent task switches.

This proposal expands on the core idea of exploiting zero-variance prompts to a more general framework for learning, where competing tasks in a multi-task setup can utilize zero-variance information effectively.

Turn 2 introduces an exciting prospect of harnessing zero-variance prompts in multi-task learning setups, but in doing so adds a level of complexity as the approach may need to balance between assisting different tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Variance Prompt Filter Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a new reinforcement learning approach that learns to select and filter out zero-variance prompts in an active manner. This is achieved by incorporating a decision module before the rollout step that evaluates the current status of learning and adjusts the level of exploration to prioritize valuable low-variance prompts. We will compare this approach to a baseline that simply filters out zero-variance prompts in a passive manner and include a control where no prompt filtering is applied. This will give us insights into whether learning to exploit or predict zero-variance prompts can lead to improved efficiency in learning.
CONTROLS: Standard GRPO, GRPO with novel prompt classification, and a baseline that filters out zero-variance prompts
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Active filtering using a learned decision module is expected to outperform standard filtering methods and may fail to learn optimal filtering strategies if the reinforcement learning signal is too weak.

This proposal introduces an exciting new direction in utilizing zero-variance prompts – learning to actively discover and utilize them in RL setups. This stands in contrast to prior methods which relied heavily on either filtering out these prompts or experimented with improved methods of leveraging them within the policy.

PROPOSAL: We propose to leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to model the temporal causal dynamics of changes in satellite imagery. TITLE: Adversarial Sampling for Thompson Sampling in Multi-Objective Linear Contextual Bandits
PROPOSAL: We develop an algorithm based on Thompson Sampling that uses a new form of optimistic sampling, which we call "adversarial sampling." Given an exponentially weighted empirical distribution over arms, we select an arm according to a probability distribution that puts positive probability on every arm. Furthermore, we construct a "worst-case context" by sampling from the prediction distribution, conditioned on the distribution of context vectors drawn so far. By taking linear combinations of the arms' rewards under this worst-case context, we create a distribution over arm values that is always upward-biased. Our algorithm then selects the arm with the highest expected value under this upward-biased distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare Adversarial Sampling to a baseline algorithm that simply draws arms from an exponentially weighted empirical distribution, which was previously proposed in the literature. We also compare to a UCB-style algorithm that uses optimistic sampling in the multi-objective setting, but which suffers from the limitations of one-at-a-time elimination.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (for running experiments and training the algorithms)
PREDICTION: We expect to demonstrate that Adversarial Sampling achieves lower Pareto regret than the baseline and UCB-style algorithm.

TITLE: Lower Bounds for Score-Based Sampling in the Low-Temperature Regime
PROPOSAL: We prove lower bounds on the error rates achievable by score-based samplers in the low-temperature regime ($\sigma \to 0$) under the manifold hypothesis. Specifically, we derive two separate bounds: one on the rate of convergence of the generated law to the manifold supported by the data, and one on the rate of convergence to the true data density on the manifold. These bounds show that accurate recovery of both the manifold geometry and the data density require different accuracy thresholds in the score function.
CONTROLS: We compare our bounds with existing convergence results for diffusion and score-based samplers, which do not distinguish between manifold geometry and data density.
COST: This proposal is a theoretical result and requires no compute.
PREDICTION: Our lower bounds will reveal the limitations of score-based sampling in the low-temperature regime and provide a rigorous foundation for future work on adapting noise schedules and improving score accuracy. We expect that achieving accurate scores in practice will be challenging, especially for large-scale generative modeling tasks.

TITLE: Contrastive Learning of Scores for Low-Temperature Smoothing
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel contrastive learning method for training score models to accurately approximate the score function of low-temperature smoothed distributions. Our approach involves training a score model to distinguish between pairs of samples that are close in the high-dimensional ambient space but far apart on the manifold, and those that are close on the manifold but far apart in the ambient space. This contrastive objective encourages the score model to capture both the geometry of the manifold and the density of the data distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to existing approaches for scoring smoothed distributions, including moment matching and score matching. We also investigate the impact of hyperparameters such as the temperature schedule and the number of training iterations on the quality of the learned scores.

PREDICTION: Our method will lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of score models for low-temperature smoothing, enabling more effective sampling and inference in high-dimensional spaces. However, we expect that small datasets and sensitive settings may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal performance. 

Relation to current proposal: Our contrastive learning objective can be seen as a practical approach to achieving the accuracy thresholds established by our lower bounds in the previous proposal.

TITLE: Hierarchical Temporal Memory with Online Sidebar for Online Multi-Step Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of Hierarchical Temporal Memory (HTM) as a base forecasting model, which is capable of modeling complex temporal patterns through its ability to remember past events. To overcome the challenges of online multi-step forecasting, we propose adding an online sidebar to the HTM, which allows the model to adapt to new data and distribution shifts during deployment. The online sidebar can be trained to predict the immediate future based on the current state of the HTM, and we can use OGD to update the entire model using the feedback from the online sidebar.

* Ablation: removing the online sidebar or the hierarchical structure of the HTM

PROPOSAL: We propose an active learning approach for online time series forecasting, where the model actively selects the most informative samples from the incoming data stream to update its parameters. TITLE: Real-Exemplar Few-Shot Refinement for Conditional Image Generators
PROPOSAL: We design and evaluate a novel few-shot refinement method, dubbed Real-Exemplar Fine-Tuning (REF), which adapts the quality and diversity of off-the-shelf conditional generators using only a small number of real exemplar images, without fine-tuning the generator. REF employs a two-stage process: (1) initial coarse alignment of the generator's distribution to the target distribution based on shape and pattern features extracted from a limited set of real exemplar images; and (2) next, iterative refinement using a generative adversarial framework with a reward function tuned to the exemplar set, incrementally expanding the set to refine progressively the generator's output. We implement REF on Cycled Generative Adversarial Network (CycleGAN) [24] using the FFHQ dataset [25].
CONTROLS: Controls will involve fine-tuning the original CycleGAN on the entire FFHQ dataset, running c-VSG [26] on an exemplar set of 5 images chosen randomly from FFHQ, and the original CycleGAN without any exemplar guidance.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: REF will demonstrate a substantial gain in diversity and an improvement in quality compared to the baseline, showing strong potential as a practical technique for conditioning generators on a small set of real images. However, we predict some challenges in scaling the method to more diverse exemplar sets and more complex task domains, and in maintaining good performance with an increasingly large number of real images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Actor-Free Q-learning with Adaptive Resolution
PROPOSAL: We explore an actor-free, value-based approach that employs a novel method to adaptively discretize the continuous action space, increasing resolution where Q-values are changing most rapidly, and refining the approximation of the Q-function using local Taylor expansions, allowing for accurate and efficient maximization of Q-values in the high-dimensional action space.
CONTROLS: Baseline performance compared against standard Q-learning and DDQN on a variety of synthetic tasks with continuous action spaces in 2D and 3D spaces.
COST: 10,000
PREDICTION: We expect this method to outperform standard Q-learning in terms of sample efficiency and convergence rate on challenging tasks with complex reward landscapes, but may struggle in cases where the action space has markedly different scales or units, causing the local approximation to lose accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions for Efficient Value-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We propose differentiable conditional compressions that dynamically reduce the dimensionality of the action space during the maximization process, leveraging spatial hierarchy and statistical structure in the Q-function to efficiently find the optimal actions without sacrificing accuracy. This approach uses lossy compression, strategically focusing computation on the most critical regions of the action space, which can then be refined using a Newton-like search step.
CONTROLS: Baseline performance comparison against existing methods (e.g..quantized-DDQN) that also employ dimensionality reduction and a reevaluation of our previous adaptive resolution approach without the additional compression step.
COST: 15,000
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to outperform existing methods in computationally expensive tasks where precision is most crucial, but may experience decreased accuracy or efficiency in sceneries where the hierarchical structure of the Q-function is poorly understood or changes frequently.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Differentiable Conditional Compressions for Efficient Value-Based Methods
PROPOSAL: We modify the differentiable conditional compressions to incorporate principles from topological data analysis to better capture the action space's underlying structure. Specifically, we represent the Q-function approximation as a simplicial complex where critical regions in the action space are identified and refined separately. This approach enables the algorithm to adapt more effectively to the changing reward landscape and identify optimal actions in high-dimensional action spaces.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies exploring the influence of different topological representations on task performance and evaluation of our previous compressions and adaptive resolution approach against the new topological compression method.
COST: 18,000
PREDICTION: We anticipate this updated compression approach to demonstrate improved sample efficiency and convergence rates over existing methods, especially in multicopters, by simultaneously exploiting the structural knowledge and adaptability, but may experience increased instability when there is little structural topology to learn from.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Topological Partitioning for Efficient Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff
PROPOSAL: We introduce a method that uses topological partitioning to divide the action space into separate regions for exploration and exploitation. In areas with high uncertainty or sparse rewards, we allocate more exploration effort, while in regions with high confidence or dense rewards, we focus on exploitation. This partitioning adapts to the changing Q-function landscape, reducing the need for exhaustive search and sample collection in high-dimensional action spaces.
CONTROLS: Comparison against existing exploration-exploitation methods (e.g., ε-greedy, entropy-based exploration) and a review of our adaptive resolution and compression approaches for relevance in exploration tasks.
COST: 16,000
PREDICTION: This method should demonstrate improved sample efficiency and balancing of exploration and exploitation, reducing the need for extensive tuning of hyperparameters, but may fail to adapt well in cases where the reward landscape changes rapidly or lacks clear structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Representation Learning for Action Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical representation learning approach that embeds the action space into a lower-dimensional manifold, where the Q-function is more distributed and easier to approximate. This hierarchical representation enables us to efficiently compute the maximizer of the Q-function, especially when the action space has complex, high-dimensional structure. The learned manifold also captures the intrinsic structure of the action space, allowing for more accurate and efficient policy evaluation.
CONTROLS: Comparison against the cross-entropy method and evolutionary strategies for action space search, as well as ablation studies on the impact of different manifold learning techniques and the quality of hierarchy construction.
COST: 22,000
PREDICTION: This approach should exhibit improved performance in complex, high-dimensional action spaces and provide accurate policy evaluation, but may struggle when the manifold learning step produces suboptimal representations of the action space, or when the hierarchy does not capture the action space's intrinsic structure well.

TITLE: Investigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: We examine whether inter-modal forgetting occurs in UMGMs on real-world benchmarks, specifically on the VQA-VSGEval (Visual Question Answering and Visual Scene Generation Evaluation) dataset and the most recent COCO-Referring-Expression (Object Referencing) dataset for referring expression grounding. We train multiple UMGMs from scratch on these datasets and fine-tune them iteratively on a specific sequence of tasks (e.g., VQA on VQA-VSGEval, then Referring Expression Grounding on COCO). We compare the performance of the final model with that of an equally-sized ensemble of models that are individually fine-tuned on each task in the sequence. If the final model suffers from catastrophic forgetting, it should have inferior performance compared to the ensemble.
CONTROLS: Baseline control comparing an equally-sized ensemble of individually fine-tuned models to the iteratively fine-tuned UMGM.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We can empirically observe the inter-modal catastrophic forgetting phenomenon in UMGMs on VQA-VSGEval and COCO.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inter-Modal Forgetting Analysis in UMGMs Using Task Controls
PROPOSAL: To understand the causes of inter-modal forgetting, we design a series of UMGM fine-tuning experiments with controlled task orders on VQA-VSGEval and COCO. We alternate task fine-tuning between modality pairs (e.g., VT½: VQA-VSGEval with a half-and-half split of visual and textual data) across iterations. For example, iteration 1 could involve fine-tuning on text-to-image generation, iteration 2 on VQA, iteration 3 on referring expression grounding, and so forth. This controlled task order allows us to pinpoint inter-modal forgetting in specific task pairs, and supports isolating contributing factors through analysis of model weights, knowledge retention, and evaluation on unseen tasks. We compare these controlled designs to random task orders for added context.
CONTROLS: Comparison to entirely random task order UMGM fine-tuning and full-environment pretraining (aligned baseline of efficacy).
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Inter-modal forgetting is strongest between text-to-image generation and VQA on both benchmarks. When UMGMs are forced to switch between strong intra-modal taks, inter-modal performance also suffers.

PROPOSAL: We adapt the mixture-of-experts (MoE) paradigm to UMGMs for inter-modal knowledge retention. TITLE: Graph Invariant Regularizers for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of graph invariant regularizers to encourage the pre-trained GNN to capture the essential structural information of test graphs while discarding irrelevant redundancy. Specifically, we will modify the GOODAT test-time method to incorporate a graph invariant loss that regularizes the GNN's representations to be invariant under a set of graph transformations (e.g. graph sampling, node/edge permutations) that are known to preserve the semantic information of the substructures. We will train and evaluate the resulting detector on a range of molecular property prediction, drug discovery, and protein function classification tasks using real-world datasets such as ZINC, Tox21, MoleculeNet, and DTP.
CONTROLS: GOODAT baseline, Random graph invariant regularizer (to evaluate the importance of the choice of graph transformations)
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should yield improved OOD detection performance compared to the vanilla GOODAT method, particularly in cases where the test graphs have complex topological structures. However, it may require careful tuning of the graph transformations and regularization hyperparameters to avoid overfitting.

PROPOSAL: We introduce an alternative performance metric, cumulative Pareto regret, which takes into account the cumulative rewards obtained over multiple rounds. This relaxation will also enable the model to capture branched dynamics more accurately by allowing particles to split across different modes while maintaining a smooth mass allocation.

PROPOSAL: We revise the Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) algorithm to obtain a lower bound on the improvement in true reward across the entire class of rewards consistent with the assumed correlation constraint, instead of a single trusted proxy. To do this, we introduce a max-and-penalty approach that simultaneously maximizes the standard RL objective and minimizes the worst-case chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy, subject to the correlation constraint. This modification guarantees a lower bound on the improvement in true reward for any reward consistent with the correlation constraint.

TITLE: One-Step Diffusion-enhanced Lipinsk Gradient

PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical discrete loss function, which decomposes the discrete objective into a hierarchical set of tasks, each with its own distinct loss function. TITLE: Investigating Classifier-Free Guidance for Finite-Speed Kac Flows
PROPOSAL: Implement classifier-free guidance in the telegrapher equation-based Kac flow framework by adding a conditional noise schedule that depends on both the observed class label and the unconditional flow's probabilistic samples. Estimate the guidance noise by conditioning on a freeze-dim affine transformation of the flow's current samples, as commonly used in diffusion models. Then, develop a novel Lyapunov-based analysis to certify that the guidance noise keeps the guided velocity field at finite kinetic energy, by proving that the conditional flow's infinitesimal generator remains infinitesimally bounded.

TITLE: Fast, Conditional Kac-Flow Sampling via Frequent Return States
PROPOSAL: Generalize the telegrapher equation-based Kac flow framework to speed up conditioning for image generation by leveraging state features that return frequently during denoising, known as 'frequent return states'. Break down the flow into discrete stages, where each stage accesses different frequent return regions of the state space locked to class-specific conditional samples. Truncate the flow early in each stage by applying velocity-invariant pruning: dropping segments where backward-time trajectories pass close to the data points in their respective frequent return regions while having low likelihood under both the current class-sampling strategy and the flow prior, preserving samples close to real data yet significantly speeding up sampling. Evaluate the influence of truncation window size on the compromise between speedup and degradation of quality and diversity of generated samples.

TITLE: Cross-Attention Warmup for Local Cropping

TITLE: Investigating Zero-Variance Prompts with Group Reward Normalization
PROPOSAL: This experiment emulates Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) but replaces the group reward normalization with a novel approach where each rollout's reward is compared against the maximum reward in the group. If the rollout's reward equals the maximum reward (i.e., it is the best outcome), it receives a normalized reward of 1. Conversely, if it is the second-best outcome, its reward is normalized to ( max(0, 1 - 1/(n-1) ) ), where n is the size of the group. This increases the training signal for zero-variance prompts, since at least one rollout will typically have a higher reward than the rest.
CONTROLS: Comparison with the standard GRPO baseline and a version of GRPO that filters out zero-variance prompts.
COST: 50,000
PREDICTION: This approach will likely improve performance on zero-variance prompts, but may cause instability in training due to the increased output variance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rewriting Convex Mixture Attention with Learned Indexing Gates
PROPOSAL: 
We introduce a new attention-style sequence mixer that combines causal softmax attention with a learned indexing gate. The gate divides each output channel into two branches: a primary branch that follows the original convex mixture attention, and a secondary branch that reads from a learned index. Each learned index selects a past value based on channel-dependent weights and a causal softmax attention distribution over past indices. By controlling the mixing ratio between primary and secondary branches, we allow channels to flexibly adopt either the traditional convex mixture or a more selective read from memory, while maintaining parallel efficiency.
CONTROLS: Vanilla softmax attention, ablated gates (no secondary branch), uniform random gates (fixed secondary branch)
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: This modification will significantly improve the expressivity of the model, especially in tasks requiring long-range memory retrieval or context-dependent channel behavior. However, it may increase computational costs and require careful tuning of network architecture and weight initialization, especially for models with a large number of channels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Efficient Per-Channel Gating Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: 
We propose three new per-channel gating mechanisms to efficiently control the mixing ratio between primary and secondary branches in our learned indexing gate attention. The mechanisms are based on separable kernels, learned scalar weights, and attention-based weights, respectively. We evaluate their impacts on model performance, expressivity, and computational efficiency. The attention-based weights particularly show promising results, achieving a good balance between expressivity and efficiency.
CONTROLS: Uniform random gates, ablated gates, and an oracle gate ( always choosing the secondary branch) to provide a baseline comparison
COST: 7200
PREDICTION: The new per-channel gating mechanisms will further enhance the model's expressivity and flexibility, but may also introduce additional complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning.

TITLE: Refined Upper Bound for Empirical KL Divergence
PROPOSAL: We derive a novel upper bound for the empirical KL divergence between the multi-objective bandit's empirically observed distribution and a specified prior distribution. This bound is based on the included observations and enables us to efficiently estimate the probability of observing a certain multicriteria reward vector, which is crucial for scalable Thompson Sampling. To obtain our bound, we utilize the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality and derive a polynomial-sized program that recovers an approximation of the empirical distribution.
CONTROLS: UCB optimization should serve as baseline.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our upper bound can enable more efficient planning for Thompson Sampling in the multi-objective bandit while offering comparable performance to the existing upper bounds for single-objective settings. Scaling issues are predicted to arise when handling extremely diverse rewards or objectives close to unbounded cardinality.

TITLE: Scalable Thompson Sampling for Multi-Objective Bandits
PROPOSAL: Building upon our refined upper bound for empirical KL divergence, we propose a novel Thompson Sampling algorithm for the multi-objective linear contextual bandit. Our algorithm, called Scalable Multi-Objective Thompson Sampling (SMARTS), uses a parallelizable approximation of the empirical distribution to sample arms efficiently and adapt to the changing context. By leveraging our upper bound, SMARTS addresses the issue of increased complexity when handling multiple objectives. 
CONTROLS: The UCB algorithm for multi-objective bandits serves as a baseline; we also compare SMARTS with a uniform random policy for a comprehensive evaluation of its performance across diverse contexts and objectives.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SMARTS is predicted to outperform the state-of-the-art UCB algorithm in a variety of multi-objective contexts, thanks to its computational efficiency and adaptability to diverse settings. However, its performance could degrade when the number of objectives grows significantly, potentially leading to sub-optimality due to decreased adaptability.

TITLE: Counterfactual-based Lower Bound for Pareto Regret
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel, counterfactual-based lower bound for Pareto regret in multi-objective bandits. This approach compares the selection of arms by the algorithm with an ``ideal'' decision-maker that always chooses the Pareto-optimal arm. By computing the expected loss from deviating from the Pareto front, our bound highlights sub-optimality regions where the algorithm could improve and also intuitively explains the deficit-induced in cumulative rewards by employing non-Pareto optimal decisions.
CONTROLS: This counterfactual lower bound serves as a baseline against which the Pareto regret of scalable algorithms, including our CTTS variant, is compared.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our lower bound can efficiently evaluate the algorithm's suboptimality relative to an ideal decision-maker and guide the development of algorithms by amplifying regions of opportunity. Challenges might arise when adapting this lower bound to changeable conditions as contextual bandits unfold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Branched Stochastic Bridges with Conserved Mass
PROPOSAL: Develop a new type of Schrödinger bridge-like approach called "BranchingSB" that uses a centroids-based method to model the branching of populations. Specifically, BranchingSB will learn a set of centroids in the initial distribution, and for each centroid, a different set of stochastic bridges will be learned to each terminal mode, with the number of stochastic bridges corresponding to the expected number of progenitor cells in the initial population that would give rise to the observed terminal mode. The centroids will be learned using a variant of the k-means algorithm that minimizes the KL divergence between the initial distribution and the centroids.
CONTROLS: We will compare BranchingSB with the standard Schrödinger bridge approach, as well as a trivial extension of the standard approach that allows for multiple stochastic bridges per centroid (which will be referred to as "MultiSB"). We will also compare BranchingSB to a baseline that uses a ML-based approach to model the branching dynamics directly (more details to be specified in future turns).
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect BranchingSB to perform better than MultiSB in capturing the branched dynamics, and at least as well as the baseline when the terminal modes are well-separated. However, we expect BranchingSB to fail when the initial distribution is highly irregular, or when the number of terminal modes is very large.

We will also adapt the stochastic bridges to each terminal mode to the new centroids, and relearn the parameters of the bridges to minimize the KL divergence between the initial distribution and the new centroids.

TITLE: Robustifying ORPO against Correlated Proxies
PROPOSAL: This is an extension to Occupational-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO). We modify the chi-squared regularization term to account for the correlation level between the proxy and true reward, by scaling the penalty based on the assumed correlation coefficient r. Instead of using a fixed regularization strength, we introduce a proxy-aware regularization term that depends on the correlation r; this way, when the proxy is highly correlated (r close to 1) with the true reward, the regularization term is stronger, and vice versa, yielding better guarantees against reward hacking. The modified objective becomes an optimization problem involving the standard RL return plus a regularization term that scales with the correlation coefficient.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against the original ORPO and other baseline methods that do not account for the correlation level, such as standard policy optimization using the proxy reward.
COST: 2541 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our modified ORPO approach will show improvements in robustness to reward hacking for high-correlation proxies and comparable performance to ORPO for lower-correlation proxies. It might, however, lead to slightly higher variance in performance due to the introduced correlation-dependent regularization.
