PROPOSAL: A set of experiments developing and evaluating an unsupervised meta-learning approach for learning axial equivariant metanetworks, which are metanetworks that enforce equivariance with respect to axial transformations (i.e., transformations that preserve the axis along which the input is defined). This should allow us to develop metanetworks that can efficiently learn from large-scale datasets without manual labeling or supervision.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of axial equivariant metanetworks learned with our proposed unsupervised meta-learning approach to traditional supervised learning methods, as well as other meta-learning approaches, on tasks such as implicit neural representation classification and editing.
COST: 720000
PREDICTION: We expect unsupervised meta-learning to enable efficient and scalable learning of axial equivariant metanetworks, particularly for complex neural network architectures, and to open up new possibilities for axis-equivalent metanetwork research.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Attention Warm-Up for Local Cropping
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of visual tokens confusion in global-local view MLLMs, we experiment with adding a cross-attention warm-up layer that takes the question tokens and projects them onto the entire image, identifying a soft attention map of relevant regions. These regions are then cropped, resized, and passed to the global-local view MLLM in addition to the downsampled global view. This allows the model to focus on a smaller set of regions when processing the local crops, reducing the loss of relevant information.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to the standard global-local view and a variant where we add an extra layer of questioning to the local crops to help identify the relevant region within these localized views.
COST: 36000
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform the standard global-local view in fine-grained VQA, improving accuracy by 5-10 percentage points. However, the added computational cost may outweigh the benefits for very large images, leading to variable results in systems with low-end hardware.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Image Emphasis Learning for Enhanced Visual Crop Guidance
PROPOSAL: We investigate using an auxiliary image emphasis learning module to guide the cropping of the local regions. The model is trained to predict an emphasis mask for the question, which highlights the most relevant parts of the image. This emphasis mask serves as a guidance signal for cropping the local regions, encouraging the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the image. We optimize the emphasis mask jointly with the downstream model, allowing it to adapt to the questions and the visual content of the image.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to a baseline where the emphasis mask is predefined, such as a uniform mask or a mask based on object detection responses, as well as to a variant where the emphasis mask is learned but not optimized jointly with the downstream model.
COST: 108000
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the accuracy of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks by enabling it to focus on the most relevant parts of the image. However, the added complexity of the emphasis learning module may lead to overfitting if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Proposal 2: Image Emphasis Learning for Enhanced Visual Crop Guidance
PROPOSAL: We simplify the emphasis learning module and decouple it from the downstream model. Instead of jointly optimizing the emphasis mask and the model, we train the emphasis mask module independently using a separate dataset with emphasis masks annotated by humans. We then use the learned emphasis mask as a guidance signal for cropping the local regions. This approach is more interpretable and easier to train, and we expect it to maintain most of the benefits of the original approach while reducing the risk of overfitting.
CONTROLS: We compare this simplified approach to the original proposal and a baseline where the emphasis mask is predefined.
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: This revised approach should still improve the accuracy of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks but with less risk of overfitting. However, the performance may suffer if the emphasis mask learned on the separate dataset does not transfer well to the VQA tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Proposal 1: Cross-Attention Warm-Up for Local Cropping
PROPOSAL: We modify the cross-attention warm-up layer to use a bottom-up attention mechanism, where the question tokens attend to the patches in the image, rather than the other way around. This allows the model to focus on the most relevant patches in the image first, and then refine its understanding of the question in relation to those patches. We expect this change to improve the performance of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare this modified approach to the original proposal and the standard global-local view.
COST: 51200
PREDICTION: This modified approach should outperform the original proposal and the standard global-local view in fine-grained VQA, improving accuracy by 5-15 percentage points. However, the added computational cost may outweigh the benefits for very large images, leading to variable results in systems with low-end hardware.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Top-Down Visual Crop Guidance for Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: We adapt the emphasis learning module from proposal 2 to the autonomous driving domain, where the goal is to identify the most relevant regions of the image for object detection and tracking. We train the emphasis mask module on a dataset of annotated images from self-driving cars and use the learned emphasis mask to guide the cropping of the local regions. We expect this approach to improve the performance of the model on object detection and tracking tasks in this domain.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to a baseline where the emphasis mask is predefined and to a variant where the emphasis mask is learned but not optimized jointly with the downstream model.
COST: 203000
PREDICTION: This approach should improve the accuracy of the model on object detection and tracking tasks in the autonomous driving domain by enabling it to focus on the most relevant parts of the image. However, the added complexity of the emphasis learning module may lead to overfitting if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Local-Global Fusion Network for Fine-Grained VQA
PROPOSAL: We design a local-global fusion network that combines the strengths of global-view and global-local view MLLMs. The network takes the downsampled global view and the cropped local views as input, and uses a fusion module to integrate the information from both views. The fusion module is trained to attend to the most relevant regions in the local views and to focus on the relevant patches in the global view. We expect this approach to improve the performance of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks by leveraging the strengths of both global-view and global-local view MLLMs.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to the standard global-view and global-local view MLLMs, as well as to a variant where we use a simple averaging module to combine the global and local views.
COST: 121000
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform the standard global-view and global-local view MLLMs in fine-grained VQA, improving accuracy by 15-25 percentage points. However, the added complexity of the fusion module may lead to overfitting if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Anchor for Fine-Grained VQA
PROPOSAL: We introduce a visual anchor module that learns to focus on a small set of anchor regions in the image that are most relevant to the question. The anchor regions are learned through self-supervision, where the model is trained to predict a mask that highlights the anchor regions. The anchor regions are then used to guide the cropping of the local views, and the model is trained to attend to the anchor regions when processing the local views. We expect this approach to improve the performance of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks by learning to focus on the most relevant regions in the image.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach to the standard global-view and global-local view MLLMs, as well as to a variant where we use a simple attention mechanism to focus on the relevant regions.
COST: 275000
PREDICTION: This approach should outperform the standard global-view and global-local view MLLMs in fine-grained VQA, improving accuracy by 20-30 percentage points. However, the added complexity of the visual anchor module may lead to overfitting if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revision of Proposal 4: Local-Global Fusion Network for Fine-Grained VQA
PROPOSAL: We modify the local-global fusion network to use a more efficient attention mechanism, such as Performer or Linformer, to integrate the information from the global view and the local views. We also add a feedback loop that allows the model to refine its anchor regions and attention mechanism based on the performance on the downstream task. We expect this modified approach to improve the performance of the model on fine-grained VQA tasks while reducing the computational cost.
CONTROLS: We compare this modified approach to the original proposal and a baseline where we use a simple averaging module to combine the global and local views.
COST: 420000
PREDICTION: This modified approach should outperform the original proposal and the baseline in fine-grained VQA, improving accuracy by 25-35 percentage points, while reducing the computational cost by 20-30%. However, the performance may suffer if the model is not carefully regularized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Zero-Variance Prompts with Group Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm and compares the performance of a standard GRPO loss function to a modified loss function that maximizes the group reward for each prompt, even when the group has no contrasting responses.
CONTROLS: A strong baseline will be the standard GRPO implementation on the same tasks, while a more in-depth control will compare this method to a GRPO variant that uses a threshold on the group reward to target prompts with mixed outcomes. These controls will help us assess whether our modified loss function increases performance on zero-variance prompts and evaluate the effect of avoiding these prompts altogether.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: We expect the modified loss function to outperform the standard GRPO loss function on zero-variance prompts, potentially leading to more stable and efficient training on these prompts; however, we anticipate challenges in avoiding mixing with the baseline for prompts with mixed outcomes due to their more varied responses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Zero-Variance Prompt Sets for Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment studies whether groups of zero-variance prompts across different tasks can be leveraged as a multi-task learning signal to improve policy optimization. By analyzing the co-occurrence of zero-variance prompts across tasks, we propose to construct a task graph and use graph convolutional networks to aggregate information from related tasks.
CONTROLS: The baseline will be a standard multi-task GRPO implementation on the same set of tasks, while a control will involve using a random task graph to evaluate the effectiveness of task relationships in the signal. Additionally, we will compare our method to a method that samples prompt-task pairs without considering task relationships.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We foresee a potential performance boost from leveraging task relationships in zero-variance prompts, particularly when these relationships are strong and consistent; however, challenges in accounting for task dependencies might lead to overfitting or decreased generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Benefits of Zero-Variance Prompts in Deep Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: This theoretical result investigates the regularization effect that zero-variance prompts have on the policy optimization process in deep reinforcement learning. We will derive bounds on the convergence rate of the policy update and analyze how the presence of zero-variance prompts affects the sequence of policy updates, potentially leading to a more stable and efficient training process.
CONTROLS: A key control will be a comparison with the standard GRPO update, which assumes a constant variance in rewards. We will also study the impact of the proportion of zero-variance prompts in the data on the overall behavior of the algorithm.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: We anticipate that zero-variance prompts will provide a regularization effect that accelerates convergence and improves stability, but the true benefit might heavily depend on the distribution of zero-variance and varied prompts in the training set, and the robustness of the measured effect may be limited.

TITLE: Evaluating Zero-Variance Prompt GANs for Auxiliary Task Completion
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a zero-variance prompt GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) variant that generates auxiliary tasks with guaranteed diverse outcomes to complement the main task. We will train the policy to optimize the group reward on these generated auxiliary tasks and evaluate whether the auxiliary tasks improve policy performance on the main task.
CONTROLS: A baseline will be the standard GRPO implementation, and controls will involve comparing the performance with different GAN architectures and hyperparameters for generating auxiliary tasks. We will also study the effect of the proportion of generated auxiliary tasks on the overall policy performance.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: We foresee improved main task performance by leveraging diverse auxiliary tasks, but the auxiliary task generation process may impact the quality of the generated tasks, and over-reliance on these supplementary tasks might impair generalization on the target tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning a Spatial-Temporal Embedding for Multi-View Synchronization
PROPOSAL: We will design an end-to-end neural architecture that takes in asynchronous video sequences from different viewpoints and outputs a spatial-temporal embedding that captures the relative temporal offset between views. Specifically, we employ a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) that extracts features from video frames, coupled with a temporal attention mechanism to highlight the most relevant frames for synchronization. The temporal embedding will be learned concurrently with the spatial relationships between views.
CONTROLS: We will compare our architecture with various state-of-the-art methods that rely on manual annotations, audio signals, or pose estimation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed method should be able to learn a robust spatial-temporal embedding that captures the temporal relationships between views, leading to improved synchronization performance. However, it may struggle with scenes lacking prominent visual features or when the views are highly skewed, leading to a larger deviation in results.

PROPOSAL: We develop a new template-based generative model for 3D molecular design, dubbed MOLEcalculator, that samples physically realistic conformations while incorporating explicit synthesis routes. TITLE: Discriminative Graph Filters for OOD Detection
PROPOSAL: We will implement and evaluate the performance of discriminative graph filters (DGFs) in identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) graphs. A DGF is a learnable component that can be appended to a pre-trained GNN to refine the representations of the input graphs. Our hypothesis is that the DGF can selectively emphasize the distinctive structural features of the test graphs while attenuating the impact of irrelevant structural redundancy. We will train DGFs on unlabeled ID graphs and evaluate their performance on a suite of benchmarks in molecular property prediction, drug discovery, and protein function classification.

COST: 4050
PREDICTION: We expect DGFs to outperform GOODAT in OOD detection accuracy due to their ability to focus on distinctive structural features, but may fail to generalize well across datasets with diverse graph structures.

PROPOSAL: We propose the development and evaluation of a Structural Abstraction Network (SAN) for out-of-distribution graph detection. This abstraction will be used to compute a graph-level OOD score. Our hypothesis is that SAN will be more effective than existing methods in detecting OOD graphs due to its ability to explicitly handle structural redundancy.

We will investigate how our model handles challenging real-world scenarios, including scene understanding, object recognition, and depth estimation in the presence of clutter, occlusion, and varying lighting conditions. We aim to evaluate the robustness and generalizability of our method to real-world data and identify potential areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a baseline that uses a standard text-to-image model and evaluate its performance on a set of real-world tasks, including scene understanding and object recognition.
COST: 6000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our depth-aware text-to-image diffusion model to demonstrate improved performance on real-world tasks and handle challenging scenarios more effectively. However, we predict that the model may struggle when dealing with extremely complex or unusual scenes that are outside its learned domain, requiring further refinement and adaptation to achieve optimal performance.

TITLE: Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising via Normal-Vectors Predictive Autoencoder
PROPOSAL: Train an unsupervised Normal-Vectors Predictive Autoencoder (NV-PAE) on synthetic LiDAR scans of urban street scenes. The NV-PAE consists of an encoder that maps a noisy point cloud to a compressed (z) space, and a decoder that predicts normal vectors for each point in the z space. We optimize the NV-PAE using a combination of point cloud reconstruction loss and a normal vector prediction loss.
CONTROLS: Baseline: TotalDenoising ( unsupervised denoising model which uses global spatial prior), ablation study with and without normal vector loss
COST: 75 GPD

PREDICTION: We expect the NV-PAE to improve point cloud denoising performance compared to TotalDenoising, especially in terms of preserving local geometry. The use of normal vectors as a supervisory signal could improve the model's ability to capture fine-grained details. However, the model may struggle to generalize to point clouds with varying densities or noise distributions.

PROPOSAL: Extend the NV-PAE (proposal 1) with a variational autoencoder (VAE) that models the uncertainty of the denoising process. PREDICTION: We expect the uncertainty-aware VAE to improve the denoising performance and robustness of the NV-PAE, especially in scenarios with ambiguity or uncertainty in the true surface location. PROPOSAL: Use multi-task learning to train a model on both the source domain adaptation task and an auxiliary task that is related to the source domain adaptation task but different from the target domain adaptation task. Specifically, use a classification task with a different set of classes on the source domain to improve the model's ability to generalize to the target domain. Evaluate the model's performance on both the source and target domains and select the hyperparameters that minimize the difference in performance between the two domains.
CONTROLS: standard domain adaptation; multi-task learning without auxiliary task; multi-task learning with different classes on source domain but without hyperparameter selection.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the multi-task learning approach with hyperparameter selection will improve generalization to the target domain by reducing overfitting to the source domain and improving the model's ability to learn relevant features. This will help to address the distribution shift between the source and target domains and improve the overall performance of the model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: guiding the exploration with operator blocks
PROPOSAL: Train an attention-based graph neural network to learn mappings between function spaces, but incorporate operator blocks derived from the PDE dynamics as structural priors to constrain the learning space, improving data efficiency. Compare the performance of three different baselines: 1) a standard GNN with no structural priors, 2) a GNN with only physics-based inductive biases through residual terms, and 3) a graph-based solver with explicit operator blocks.
CONTROLS: (1) Standard GNN on the same task without operator blocks, (2) a GNN trained on a related but different PDE system as a form of transfer learning.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed GNN with operator blocks should outperform the standard GNN baseline, showing improved data efficiency and exploration reduction. We expect significant gains in training efficiency, especially for problems with complex geometries and boundary conditions. However, performance may suffer when the operator structure of the source term does not fit the assumed form.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  bound on free term learning
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical bound on the sample complexity required for neural PDE solvers to learn the source term $f(\mathbf{x}, t)$, given that the solver has been trained on PDE systems with similar dynamical operators $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{x}}$. Show that with a strong inductive bias towards the operator structure and sufficient data on related systems, the solver can generalize to unseen source terms with a bound on the learning rate. The bound will depend on the similarity between the PDE systems and the norm of the source term.
CONTROLS: (1) Compare the theoretical bound to empirical estimates of sample complexity using the standard GNN with no structural priors from proposal 1, (2) apply the bound to a modified setting where the source term varies across space and time but has a similar form to the one seen during training.
COST: negligible compute cost
PREDICTION: The bound should capture the empirical behavior of neural PDE solvers fairly well, and provide insights into the conditions under which they can generalize to new source terms. However, since the bound relies on strong assumptions about the similarity of PDE systems, its applicability might be limited to cases with closely related dynamics.

TITLE: attention-based hybrid aggregation

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: rooted tree sampling with the despentes nets
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of the despentes net model that learns to sample rooted tree-like digraphs. Utilize a message passing algorithm with a learned scoring function to select nodes for expansion while respecting the rooted tree structure. Implement this method on a combination of synthetic and real-world graph datasets and compare its performance to the standard despentes net and the state-of-the-art PAP HeRL model.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art model PAP HeRL and pioneer despentes net on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: estimated 4 days, approximately 1800 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the variant of the despentes net will perform competitively with PAP HeRL and better than the standard despentes net on the rooted tree-like digraph sampling task, with potential failure points in the scalability of the method on larger datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: hierarchical graph generation with spatial-aware flows
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical graph generation model that incorporates spatial-aware flows to capture the directional dependencies in directed graphs. Use a multi-scale approach to learn the graph structure, where each scale represents a different level of abstraction. Utilize a bidirectional flow mechanism that enables the model to learn both the strengths and weaknesses of the edge directions.
CONTROLS: Use the standard detangling step on the HEARJ autoencoder as a baseline, as well as the previously discussed despentes net variant.
COST: estimated 5 days, approximately 2200 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We expect this model to outperform the baselines on a variety of directed graph generation tasks, particularly in scenarios where the graph structure is hierarchical and spatially-sensitive. Potential failure points may arise if the bidirectional flow mechanism introduces additional difficulties in optimizing the model parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: connecting graph generation to neural architecture search
PROPOSAL: Investigate the connection between directed graph generation and neural architecture search (NAS). Use the hierarchical graph generation model from previous proposal to generate graphs that represent possible architectures, and then employ a search algorithm to find the optimal architecture within the generated graph space.
CONTROLS: Use the standard despentes net variant and the PAP HeRL model as baselines for the graph generation task, as well as a state-of-the-art NAS algorithm as a baseline for the search task.
COST: estimated 6 days, approximately 2800 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this model can discover novel architectures and improve the performance of the state-of-the-art NAS algorithm, with potential failure points in the scalability of the search algorithm and the quality of the generated graph space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: scene graph generation with directed graph priors
PROPOSAL: Extend the hierarchical graph generation model to generate scene graphs, where the model is trained with directed graph priors learned from a dataset of annotated scene graphs. Use a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) to learn the scene-specific graph structure and a directed graph prior to guide the generation process.
CONTROLS: Use the cVAE model as a baseline for scene graph generation, as well as the hierarchical graph generation model without the directed graph prior.
COST: estimated 7 days, approximately 3400 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We expect this model to outperform the baselines on scene graph generation tasks, particularly in scenarios where the scene-specific graph structure is complex and directional. Potential failure points may arise if the directed graph prior introduces additional difficulties in optimizing the model parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluation metrics for directed graph generative quality
PROPOSAL: Investigate and propose new evaluation metrics to assess the quality of directed graph generators. Compare the performance of various graph generators using a set of established metrics, such as graph similarity, structure, and edge direction consistency, as well as novel metrics that capture the complexity and topological features of directed graphs.
CONTROLS: Use the previously proposed graph generators (1-5) as a baseline for the evaluation task.
COST: estimated 2 days, approximately 800 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this work will shed light on the limitations of current evaluation metrics and inspire the development of more robust and interpretable methods to assess the performance of directed graph generators. Potential failure points may arise if the novel metrics are not effectively capture the underlying graph structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: experimental digraphs through gradamory helpers
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of grammar-based approaches to generate directed graphs, where a set of production rules are used to construct graphs that fit specific patterns or structures. Utilize a variant of the Context-Free Grammar (CFG) to generate directed graphs with specific properties, such as acyclicity or connectivity.
CONTROLS: Use the standard despentes net variant and the PAP HeRL model as baselines for comparison.
COST: estimated 8 days, approximately 4400 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64) 
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to be effective in generating graphs with specific properties, but may require significant tuning of the grammar rules to achieve high-quality results. Potential failure points may arise if the grammar rules are too restrictive or too permissive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: comprehensive benchmark for directed graph generation
PROPOSAL: Establish a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating directed graph generation models, including a suite of tasks, datasets, and evaluation metrics. This benchmark will enable researchers to compare the performance of different graph generation models and identify areas for improvement. Utilize the previously proposed graph generators (1-7) as a starting point for the benchmark.
CONTROLS: Use the standard PAP HeRL model and the despentes net variant as baselines for comparison.
COST: estimated 5 days, approximately 2500 GPU-hours (P100 batch size of 64)

Potential failure points may arise if the benchmark is not effective in capturing the complexity of the tasks or if the evaluation metrics are not aligned with the needs of real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: scalable flow-based schrödinger bridge solver
PROPOSAL: develop a scalable flow-based Schrödinger bridge (SB) solver for the tree-structured SB problem, extending the Iterative Markovian Fitting (IMF) scheme to handle the tree structure while ensuring convergence to the tree-structured SB solution, using a neural network to parameterise the SB map and stochastically compute the optimal flow through the tree.
CONTROLS: ablate the tree structure by comparing performance with the original IMF scheme applied to a sequence-structured SB problem, ablate the neural network parameterisation and compare with a non-parametric compute of the SB map.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the scalable IMF scheme will converge to the tree-structured SB solution in significantly fewer iterations than the original sequence-structured IMF scheme, and outperform existing solvers for entropic Wasserstein barycentres in terms of computational efficiency, but may suffer from numerical instability or mode collapse in high-dimensional settings.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: scalable flow-based schrödinger bridge solver

CONTROLS: compare the revised solver with a non-parametric proposal distribution, ablate the learnable proposal distribution and compare with a fixed proposal distribution.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (adds 500 GPU-hours for training the learnable proposal distribution)
PREDICTION: the revised solver will exhibit improved numerical stability and robustness to mode collapse in high-dimensional settings, and outperform existing solvers in terms of efficiency and accuracy, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for the learnable proposal distribution.

ACTION: ADD
title: exploring relaxed equivariance in metanetworks
proposal: propose a theoretical framework that characterizes the properties of metanetworks that guarantee functional equivalence preservation, under a definition of relaxed or approximate equivariance. the framework should consider the symmetries of the processed architecture, such as permutations, scaling, and sign changes, and provide a mathematical characterization of the optimal trade-offs between expressivity and symmetry preservation.
controls: ablation of strict equivariance requirement, comparison with existing metanetwork architectures that enforce strict equivariance.
cost: 10 gpu-hours.
prediction: the theoretical framework should reveal the feasibility of relaxing strict equivariance in metanetworks, with a balance that depends on the specific symmetry group of the architecture being processed. this could open up new directions for designing more expressive metanetworks that preserve functional equivalence.

ACTION: ADD
title: analysis of equivariance in layered perceptrons
proposal: design a theoretical study that analyzes the equivariance properties of layered perceptrons, specifically exploring how the layers interact and contribute to the overall equivariance of the network. this will help in understanding how the strict equivariance requirement in metanetworks can be relaxed at the layer-wise level.
controls: comparison with previous work on equivariance in single-layer perceptrons, assessment of the impact of activation functions on equivariance.
cost: 20 gpu-hours.
prediction: the analysis will reveal that some layers are more amenable to relaxed equivariance than others, and that the choice of activation function can significantly impact the equivariance properties of the network. this will inform the design of more flexible metanetwork architectures.

ACTION: ADD
title: autoeg equivariant metanetwork architecture
proposal: propose a novel metanetwork architecture, AUTOEG, that learns to automatically adapt its equivariance structure to the processed network weights. AUTOEG will consist of an equivariant encoder that captures the symmetries of the input weights, followed by a differentiable group predictor that learns to predict the correct group action for each input.
controls: comparison with existing metanetwork architectures that require manual specification of equivariance groups, assessment of the impact of encoder and predictor architectures on the overall performance.
cost: 100 gpu-hours.
prediction: AUTOEG will be able to effectively learn and adapt to the equivariance properties of various network architectures, outperforming or matching the performance of state-of-the-art metanetwork architectures.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
title: autoeg equivariant metanetwork architecture
proposal: revise the AUTOEG architecture to incorporate a learnable penalty term for equivariance violations, allowing the model to trade-off equivariance and expressivity. the penalty term will be computed based on the estimated group action and the actual input weights, and will be optimized jointly with the regular metanetwork loss.
controls: ablation study on the impact of the penalty term, comparison with existing metanetwork architectures that enforce strict equivariance.
cost: 120 gpu-hours.
prediction: the revised AUTOEG architecture will be able to balance equivariance and expressivity more effectively, leading to better performance on various metanetwork tasks, and will provide insights into the importance of equivariance in metanetworks.

ACTION: REVISE
number: 3
title: autoeg equivariant metanetwork architecture
proposal: revise the AUTOEG architecture to incorporate a learnable penalty term for equivariance violations, allowing the model to trade-off equivariance and expressivity. the penalty term will be computed based on the estimated group action and the actual input weights, and will be optimized jointly with the regular metanetwork loss. additionally, modify the architecture to include an auxiliary loss for predicting the correct function equivalence class of the input weights.
controls: ablation study on the impact of the penalty term and auxiliary loss, comparison with existing metanetwork architectures that enforce strict equivariance.

title: analysis of equivariance in layered perceptrons

controls: comparison with a variant of the analysis that does not take into account residual connections, assessment of the impact of different residual connection strategies on equivariance.
cost: 80 gpu-hours.
prediction: the analysis will reveal that residual connections can either enhance or compromise equivariance, depending on their implementation and the architecture of the layer. this will provide valuable insights for designing more equivariant neural networks.

ACTION: ADD
title: graph neural network-based metanetworks
proposal: propose a novel metanetwork architecture that utilizes graph neural networks (GNNs) to model the relationships between neurons and weight matrices. the GNN will learn to represent the graph structure of the input weights and adapt its equivariance properties accordingly.
controls: comparison with existing metanetwork architectures, assessment of the impact of different GNN architectures and graph structures on metanetwork performance.

prediction: the GNN-based metanetwork architecture will be able to effectively capture the structural relationships between weights and neurons, leading to better performance on various metanetwork tasks.

ACTION: ADD
title: weight-space-based implicit neural representation classification
proposal: propose a novel method for classification of implicit neural representations based on weight-space embeddings. the method will utilize a contrastive loss to learn a discriminative embedding of weights that captures the semantic differences between neural networks.
controls: comparison with existing methods for implicit neural representation classification, assessment of the impact of different weight-space embeddings and contrastive loss functions on classification accuracy.
cost: 200 gpu-hours.
prediction: the weight-space-based method will be able to effectively capture the semantic differences between neural networks, leading to better classification accuracy and providing new insights into the properties of implicit neural representations.

ACTION: ADD
title: evaluating metanetworks with neural network generalization prediction from weights

controls: comparison with existing methods for generalization prediction, assessment of the impact of different metanetwork architectures and hyperparameters on prediction accuracy.
cost: 250 gpu-hours.
prediction: the benchmarking study will reveal the strengths and limitations of metanetwork-based generalization prediction, providing insights into the potential applications and limitations of these methods in practice.

ACTION: ADD
title: unsupervised learning of metanetworks for implicit neural representation editing
proposal: propose a method for unsupervised learning of metanetworks that can edit implicit neural representations by learning to manipulate the weights of the original neural network. the method will utilize a variational autoencoder to learn a probabilistic representation of the weights and a metanetwork to predict the edited weights.
controls: comparison with existing methods for implicit neural representation editing, assessment of the impact of different metanetwork architectures and variational autoencoder configurations on editing quality.
cost: 300 gpu-hours.
prediction: the unsupervised learning method will enable efficient and accurate editing of implicit neural representations, opening up new possibilities for applications in computer vision, graphics, and other fields.

TITLE: region-sensitive attention masking
PROPOSAL: adaptively mask out irrelevant regions in the input image based on the question context and the attention patterns of the MLLM. This is achieved by iteratively selecting a subset of the image tokens based on relevance scores, which are updated as the model processes more tokens. The model is thus guided to focus on the most relevant regions, reducing information loss and improving performance on fine-grained VQA.
CONTROLS: standard global-view and global-local-view MLLMs, ablated model with fixed attention mask
COST: low (estimated 200 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: significantly improved performance on fine-grained VQA tasks, reduced computational cost due to reduced attention footprint. likely to benefit remaining experimental frameworks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: sparse permutation attention
PROPOSAL: We develop Sparse Permutation Attention (SPA), a sparse attention mechanism that selects a subset of input indices for each query. SPA uses a sparse permutation matrix to select a subset of input indexes, which are then used to compute the output. In SPA, the permutation matrix is computed using a standard attention mechanism, but with a sparse output. We compare SPA to standard softmax attention on a variety of sequence-to-sequence tasks and show that it can significantly reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy.
CONTROLS: Softmax attention, sparse attention with diagonal masking
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SPA should significantly outperform standard softmax attention in terms of computational efficiency, and show comparable or better accuracy on sequence-to-sequence tasks. However, the performance may degrade on tasks with a large number of inputs and outputs.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: subquery attention
PROPOSAL: We propose Subquery Attention, a mechanism that allows each query to access specific values from different input indices. Subquery Attention uses a query mechanism to identify a subset of input indices for each query and then applies a secondary attention mechanism to these selected indices. We compare Subquery Attention to standard softmax attention and sparse attention on sequence-to-sequence tasks and show that it can significantly improve accuracy on tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing.
CONTROLS: Softmax attention, sparse permutation attention, softmax attention with subquery mechanism (ablation study)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Subquery Attention should show significant improvements in accuracy on sequence-to-sequence tasks with non-sequential or irregular timestep indexing, and outperform sparse permutation attention in terms of accuracy. However, the performance may degrade on tasks with a large number of inputs and outputs due to increased computational cost.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: sparse permutation attention
REVISED PROPOSAL: We develop Sparse Permutation Attention (SPA), a sparse attention mechanism that selects a subset of input indices for each query. SPA uses a sparse permutation matrix to select a subset of input indexes, which are then used to compute the output. We modify SPA to incorporate subspace screening, where we use a separate attention mechanism to identify the relevant subspaces of the input data, which are then used to compute the permutation matrix. We compare SPA with subspace screening to standard softmax attention, sparse attention, and subquery attention on sequence-to-sequence tasks and show that it can significantly improve accuracy and reduce computational cost.

PROPOSAL: modify the one-hot encoding by representing each class as a ball in a multi-dimensional space, where each dimension corresponds to a class. The pseudo-label of a pixel is represented as a weighted sum of these class balls, with weights given by the softmax output of the model. This creates a probabilistic representation of the class that captures the uncertainty and ambiguity between classes.
CONTROLS: ablation study of one-hot vs. ball representation, sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters governing the weight of each class ball, comparison with existing filter-out mechanisms and weighting functions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: the uncertain representation is expected to be more informative than one-hot labels and should provide better robustness to label noise, but its performance may suffer from over-smoothing due to the probabilistic nature of the representation.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: class kernel coding
PROPOSAL: replace the one-hot encoding with a kernel representation of each class. Compute a set of class kernels using the activations of the classification layer, and use a weighted sum of these kernels to represent the pseudo-label of a pixel. The weights are given by the softmax output of the model.
CONTROLS: comparison with uncertainty-aware pseudo-label coding, comparison with existing weighting functions and filter-out mechanisms, ablation study of the choice of kernels and their weights. Also, this experiment requires a kernel learning strategy, such as Nystrom approximation or kernel dictionary learning.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this representation is expected to capture the shared attributes between confusing classes, but its performance may suffer from vibrations and instability due to the high dimensionality of the kernel space.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: context-dependent pseudo-label encoding
PROPOSAL: adapt the pseudo-label encoding to the local context of each pixel. Use a segmentation model to obtain a set of context-dependent 'atoms' or binary features that capture the relevance of each class in different parts of the image. Represent the pseudo-label of a pixel as a weighted sum of these atoms, where the weights are given by the output of the segmentation model.
CONTROLS: comparison with uncertainty-aware pseudo-label coding and class kernel coding, ablation study of the choice of atoms and their weights, evaluation on a range of segmentation tasks and datasets.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this encoding should provide better robustness to mislabeling and adaptability to different contexts, but its performance may suffer from over-complicated representation and computations required for obtaining the context-dependent atoms.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: spatial-temporal attention-based pseudo-label encoding
PROPOSAL: replace the context-dependent atom representation with a spatial-temporal attention mechanism. Use the segmentation model to compute a set of attentive weights that highlight the relevant regions and time-steps for each class. Represent the pseudo-label of a pixel as a weighted sum of the output of the segmentation model, where the weights are given by the attentive weights computed for each class.
CONTROLS: comparison with uncertainty-aware pseudo-label coding and class kernel coding, ablation study of the choice of attention weights and their computation, evaluation on a range of segmentation tasks and datasets.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: this encoding should provide more flexible and adaptive representation than the context-dependent atom representation, but its performance may suffer from overfitting to the specific time-steps and regions used for attention computation.

ACTION: ADD 6

This approach can improve the quality of the pseudo-labels by leveraging the knowledge of the teacher model.
CONTROLS: comparison with using the teacher model's predictions directly as pseudo-labels, ablation study of the choice of teacher and student models, evaluation on a range of segmentation tasks and datasets.

TITLE: practical bounds for wide neural networks
PROPOSAL: We will derive a new bound on the generalization error of wide neural networks based on the spectral norm of the Jacobian of the forward pass, and show that for certain classification problems with NTK-separable data, the risk of large over-parameterized neural networks can be bounded by $\widetilde{O}(1/(n\gamma^2))$, matching the minimax optimal rate established in the kernel setting, with no exponential dependence on the depth $L$.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: stochastic particle branch characterisation
PROPOSAL: Develop a new stochastic particle method, which we call the "branch-characterising Brownian motion" (BCBM). In BCBM, each particle has a branching probability, allowing it to split into multiple offspring particles or merge with other particles. The splitting and merging rules are designed such that the mass of the particle cloud under the BCBM dynamics matches the target branching distribution. We will then use the BCBM to continuously estimate the branching probability and transition densities between different modes of the target distribution.
CONTROLS: We will compare the BCBM to standard methods such as the current generalized Schrödinger bridge formulation, as well as a diffusion-based method with explicit branching dynamics (such as the branching Brownian motion). For the latter, we will compare our method's ability to accurately predict the time of branching and mass redistribution between modes.
COST: Estimated compute: 3k GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The BCBM should successfully capture the branching dynamics and estimate the mass redistribution between modes more accurately than existing methods, especially when the branching is non-linear or has multiple modes. However, it may be computationally expensive and hard to tune, especially for very large-scale datasets.

TITLE: incremental learning of go strategies through game play
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our LLM on learning Go strategies through incremental learning, where it's presented with a sequence of games and must incrementally update its knowledge and strategies. We'll use a dataset of Go games, where the model's performance is evaluated at regular intervals during the game sequence. We'll compare the model's performance to human annotators and evaluate its ability to learn and adapt to new situations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Model performance on learning Go strategies through few-shot learning and policy distillation; comparison to human annotators' performance on incremental learning tasks.
COST: Approximately 25,000 - 35,000 GPU hours, depending on the length of the game sequence and the complexity of the strategies.
PREDICTION: We anticipate significant improvement in the model's ability to learn and adapt to new situations, with a corresponding increase in its ability to reason about Go positions and strategies. However, we also risk encountering difficulties in aligning the model's learned strategies with the expert examples.

TITLE: human-like go commentary generation at scale
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of our LLM on generating human-like Go commentary at scale, using a large dataset of Go games and a evaluation metric that focuses on the coherence, completeness, and accuracy of the commentary. We'll compare the model's performance to human annotators and evaluate its ability to produce high-quality commentary for a large number of games.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Model performance on generating Go commentary through multimodal evaluation and policy distillation; comparison to human annotators' performance on human-like go commentary generation.
COST: Approximately 40,000 - 50,000 GPU hours, depending on the size of the dataset and the complexity of the commentary.
PREDICTION: We anticipate significant improvement in the model's ability to generate human-like Go commentary at scale, with a corresponding increase in its ability to reason about Go positions and strategies. However, we also risk encountering difficulties in aligning the model's commentary with the expert examples. This will be the final task to help close the gap between general LLMs and the Go expert level.
